verifyArtProtocol.blindIdentification: The verifier is shown the render with no filename and no label and must name the subject unprompted. That answer is recorded first.
verifyArtProtocol.then: Only then is the render compared against `referenceFiles` and `mustBeRight` for that subject.
verifyArtProtocol.pass: The unprompted identification matches `subject` AND every entry in `mustBeRight` is present.
verifyArtProtocol.fail: Recognisable only once you know what it is, any missing `mustBeRight` entry, or any entry from `neverAdd` present.
whichFileAnswersWhichSubject: `renders` on each subject is the answer, and it exists because without it the same image passed one
subject and failed another and there was no way to say which verdict counted. A subject with an empty
`renders` is UNRENDERED, not failed: no image is judged against it and its lists are dormant.
`renderRecipe` says how to build the image. A single-file subject is that file rasterised. A CHARACTER
cannot be judged from any single file: it is a rig of separate parts and every one of them is
unidentifiable alone. Its recipe names the parts, their draw order and the slot choices, all of which
come from assets/style/rig-contract.json - the parts list, the z order and the frame templates.
verifyArtProtocol.contradictionRule: An entry in one subject's `neverAdd` may not forbid an entry in another subject's `mustBeRight`. Where two subjects cover overlapping geometry, the narrower prohibition wins and is scoped in its own text.
anonymisedHandOff: An identifier that finds its own inputs has already read their filenames, so it is not blind.
The rasterise-and-rename step must be run by something the identifier does not run, and the identifier
must be handed image bytes with a neutral name and no directory listing. Recorded here after a pass
marked all of its own verdicts untrusted for exactly this reason, which was the right call.

subjects.subject: The Peace Tower, Centre Block, Parliament Hill, Ottawa
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers.

mustBeRight.feature: green copper spire
mustBeRight.why: The single strongest colour cue. A tall pale-green pyramidal spire on a pale stone tower is the Peace Tower and almost nothing else.
mustBeRight.detail: Steep square-based pyramid, apex angle about 26 degrees, oxidised copper green. MEASURED 2026-09-08: the spire is 0.21 of the tower height in peace-tower-elevation.jpg and 0.18 in officer-and-peace-tower-portrait.jpg. The 'about 30 percent' this entry carried until then was never measured and was wrong; it is corrected rather than kept, because a render built to it would put the spire base through the clock. Spire base width is 0.75 of the shaft width. Anything under 0.15 of the tower height stops reading as the Peace Tower.

mustBeRight.feature: clock face
mustBeRight.why: Named in the brief and in every photograph a learner has seen. Without it the tower is a generic Gothic spire.
mustBeRight.detail: One large circular white clock face centred on the tower shaft, just below the belfry stage. MEASURED: centre at 0.74 of the tower height above the terrace (0.62 was recorded here before measurement and was wrong), dial diameter 0.40 of the shaft width. Dark surround, dark hands. DELIBERATE EXAGGERATION: the shipped art draws the dial at 0.55 of the shaft width and centres it at 0.72, because the shipped shaft is 113 px wide at design resolution, so a true 0.40 dial is 45 px there and about 16 px on a phone held at arm's length, where it stops being a clock and becomes a white dot. MEASURED, and the third figure in this file that was asserted before it was measured: the quantity is the dial ON A PHONE, not at design resolution. Exaggerating an identifying feature is simplification (art-bible section 5, rule 2); this is the only feature on this subject that is exaggerated, and the spire is NOT, so the two do not collide.

mustBeRight.feature: national flag on the mast above the spire
mustBeRight.detail: A single flagpole rising from the spire apex, flying the National Flag of Canada. The flag reads at small size only if it is drawn at least 40 px wide at design resolution.
mustBeRight.whyMasked: MEASURED against the shipped 1080x1040 render: the flag and its mast occupy rows 2-123, and the copper spire's apex begins at row 125, so this rectangle removes the flag and leaves every other feature intact. A hand pass found masking the flag dropped identification from about 0.90 to about 0.65, and on a tower crop it failed outright - 'a Big Ben-like Gothic clock tower'. That is the most useful single fact anyone has measured about this subject and it had no way to be re-measured. Now it does. DIAGNOSTIC, never gating: a subject leaning on one strong cue is information, not a defect.

mustBeRight.feature: pale warm sandstone shaft
mustBeRight.detail: Nepean sandstone, warm buff. Use the `stone` ramp. Not grey, not white.

mustBeRight.feature: tall pointed arch at the base
mustBeRight.detail: One large Gothic arched entrance at the foot of the tower, on the tower's centre line. This is the Memorial Arch entrance.

mustBeRight.feature: tower rises from the centre of a symmetrical wing block
mustBeRight.detail: Centre Block's two wings run left and right from the tower base at roughly one third of the tower height. The composition is symmetrical about the tower.

mustBeRight.feature: vertical proportion
mustBeRight.detail: The tower reads as slender: shaft width to total height. MEASURED 1:6.8 in peace-tower-elevation.jpg (a telephoto from below, foreshortened at the base) and 1:8.5 in officer-and-peace-tower-portrait.jpg; the building itself is about 1:7.6 (92.2 m tall on a 12.2 m square shaft). The shipped art is 880 x 113 = 1:7.8. Anything squatter than 1:6 stops being the Peace Tower.

simplifyAway: stone coursing and masonry joints
window tracery and mullions
gargoyles and grotesques
carved figures and heraldry over the arch
dormers and chimneys under 8 px at design resolution
the corner turrets' finials
Roman numerals on the dial: below 6 px at design resolution, so they become four cardinal tick marks. Rhythm replacing count, not an invented ornament (art-bible section 5, rule 3)
the eleven-point outline of the maple leaf on the flag: at a 59 px flag the notches are 3 px, so the leaf is drawn as a bold five-lobe silhouette
neverAdd: a second tower or spire ON THE PEACE TOWER ITSELF, and no twin tower flanking it. SCOPED 2026-09-08: this read as a blanket ban on any other roofline on the Hill, which contradicted parliament-hill-skyline's mustBeRight entry for the Library of Parliament's polygonal roof - a real building that the shipped render draws and that its own <title> names. A neverAdd on one subject may not forbid a mustBeRight on another; that contradiction is what makes a literal verifier fail a render for drawing a required feature.
a dome
round or rose windows
battlements or crenellation on the tower shaft
a clock face on more than the visible faces
a bell visible in the belfry openings
notes: Centre Block has been under rehabilitation since 2019. `centre-block-front-elevation.jpg` and
`parliament-hill-skyline-sunset.jpg` show cranes, hoarding and scaffolding, and the wing roofs
stripped to dark metal. Draw the building in its settled state: green copper wing roofs, no
cranes, no hoarding. `parliament-hill-skyline.jpg` shows that state. See OQ-ART-05.
`peace-tower-clock-face.jpg` is a night exposure with a purple cast; use it for the dial layout
and the numeral style, not for colour.

peace-tower-clock-daylight.jpg (CC BY 2.0, added 2026-09-08 once the credits enum could express the licence) is the daylight dial: use it for the dial layout, the surround and the belfry, not peace-tower-clock-face.jpg, which is a night exposure with a purple cast.

officer-and-peace-tower-portrait.jpg is public domain and frames the whole composition this level wants - Centre Block symmetrical about the tower, green copper wing roofs intact, seen from the lawn. It predates 1965, so the mast flies the Canadian Red Ensign; the level draws the National Flag of Canada.
PLACEMENT FLOOR, from the size ladder: do not draw this landmark below 300 px wide anywhere the player
is meant to recognise it. Measured cold - 0.92 at full size, 0.88 at 300 px, 0.75 at 140 px, where the
dial has collapsed to a pale disc with a dark rim and the Gothic arcade to texture, leaving the flag and
the copper green carrying it almost alone. This is a level-design constraint, not a drawing one: no
amount of redrawing buys back a 62 px dial rendered at 8 px.
The 1x source pin was checked before it was accepted and passed cold at 0.92 with the verifier's own
verdict recorded: it does not need 2x back.

subjects.subject: The Rideau Canal Skateway, Ottawa, in winter
expectedBlindAnswer: an outdoor skating rink on a frozen canal
skating on a frozen urban canal

mustBeRight.feature: the ice lane is contained by built edges, not by a natural shore
mustBeRight.why: This is a canal, not a pond or a lake. The containment is the whole read. It was written as 'two low retaining walls running to the vanishing point', which is a view down the canal; TrueNorth is a side-scroller and looks ACROSS it, where that view does not exist. Amended 2026-09-08 so the contract describes what the shipped camera can show.
mustBeRight.detail: In the side view the containment reads as: one low masonry retaining wall running the full width behind the ice with snow banked against its foot, an iron railing along its head, and a near snow bank framing the bottom of the frame. Ice fills everything between them. Straight, level, parallel edges - a built channel, never a curved shoreline.

mustBeRight.feature: scored skate marks in the ice
mustBeRight.detail: Fine curved white scratches across the ice surface. Draw them as a sparse repeating overlay in `snow-light` at low opacity, never as noise.

mustBeRight.feature: people skating, not walking
mustBeRight.detail: Skate blades under the boots, glide stance with the trailing leg extended, arms low. Winter coats, toques, mitts.

mustBeRight.feature: a road bridge crossing overhead
mustBeRight.detail: The skateway passes under low bridges. At least one crossing bridge should be visible in the level's horizontal run; it is the strongest depth cue the canal gives.

mustBeRight.feature: cold overcast or low winter light
mustBeRight.detail: Ice is not white. Use the `ice` ramp against `snow` banks so the lane reads as a distinct surface.

simplifyAway: individual bricks in the retaining wall
street furniture above the wall line
distant office towers
neverAdd: a hockey rink, boards, nets or line markings
a natural shoreline with reeds or rocks: this is a built canal
mountains or hills on the horizon
notes: `rideau-canal-ottawa-locks.jpg` shows the flight of locks at the Ottawa River end with the
Chateau Laurier above. Use it for lock-gate geometry and canal masonry only. The Chateau
Laurier is not a slice-1 subject and should not be drawn as a recognisable landmark here.
`rideau-canal-skateway-portrait.jpg` is the closest reference to the shipped aspect ratio and
is the primary composition reference for the level.
The road bridge is drawn end-on, because a bridge crossing the canal is seen as a portal the skater passes through when the camera looks across the canal rather than along it.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: AMENDED 2026-09-08. This list used to require 'Rideau Canal' or 'skating on a frozen canal in Ottawa',
and the render contains no Ottawa cue at all. The first honest blind pass matched it anyway, at 0.60, and
said so in its own answer: 'I am naming it from the genre, not from a unique landmark in the picture.' It
inferred the intent from project context. A verifier without that context answers 'an urban frozen-canal
skating rink' and fails a gate that the art satisfies. A contract that demands more than the art is
allowed to show fails an honest verifier and passes a compliant one, which is the wrong way round.
So the generic answers now PASS, and the two specific ones stay in the list because they are still
correct - a verifier that names the Rideau Canal is not wrong, it is just not required to.
WHY NO OTTAWA CUE IS COMING. This is not a drawing that could be improved. The subject's render is
`layer-50-canalwall` over `layer-60-ice`, and BOTH ARE REPEATING PARALLAX TILES - 2016 px and 1440 px.
A unique landmark drawn on a repeating tile appears three times across the level, so the Chateau Laurier
instruction in `notes` is a consequence of the tiling, not a scope decision that could be reversed. The
same rule blocks the locks, the Parliament silhouette and anything else that names a city. And the tile
is the one that must survive the `low` preset dropping to two layers, so a cue cannot be exiled to a
droppable layer either.
WHERE OTTAWA ACTUALLY COMES FROM. The level composite: `ottawa-landmark-parliament-hill`, a separate,
non-repeating subject that identified cold at 0.92. The canal is where the player skates; the Hill is
what says which country and which city. Splitting them across two subjects is what lets each one be
judged on what it actually contains.

subjects.subject: A canal lock with closed timber gates, in winter
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`, the same builder as peace-tower.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. A lock chamber is a lock chamber; it names no canal and no city, and the gate
must not ask it to. The place-anchor for this level is parliament-hill.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY IS THE MECHANISM. "A dam", "a weir", "a bridge", "a wall" or "a dock" is a FAIL.
The pair of gates meeting at a mitre, with a long balance beam swung out over each wall, is what a
lock has and none of those has.

mustBeRight.feature: a pair of gates meeting at a mitre across the chamber, pointing at the viewer
mustBeRight.why: It is the whole subject. A single flat gate across a channel is a sluice; two leaves meeting at an angle is a lock, and the angle is what makes the gates hold against the water behind them.
mustBeRight.detail: Two leaves, each running from its own wall to the centre, meeting on a vertical seam. The near edge of each leaf is LOWER on screen at the centre than at the wall, which is what draws the mitre pointing toward the camera. Each leaf carries three horizontal rails in a lighter tone of the same material.

mustBeRight.feature: a long balance beam swung out over each wall from the head of each gate
mustBeRight.why: It is the second half of the mechanism and the strongest horizontal in the picture. In the reference both beams are white timber and they are the only thing in the frame at that angle.
mustBeRight.detail: A tapering beam from the gate head out across the coping, ending over the wall, with a dark pivot block where the two gate heads meet. Drawn white with a lit top edge. They are what a person reads as "somebody pushes this open".

mustBeRight.feature: coursed stone chamber walls either side, with a coping and snow on top
mustBeRight.detail: Two masonry piers framing the chamber, each with four or five course lines and a few staggered vertical joints, a projecting coping course, and a band of `snow` above it with a lit crest. The first build drew the courses in the shade tone at 7 px and the wall read as brickwork; they are drawn in the base tone against a light face now.

mustBeRight.feature: a black iron handrail along the top of each wall
mustBeRight.detail: Two posts and two rails per wall, in a dark neutral, standing clear against the sky. It is what says a person can stand here, and it is in the reference.

mustBeRight.feature: ice in the chamber, not water, and no boat
mustBeRight.why: This level is winter and its locomotion is skating. Falling water in the frame would put the level in the wrong season.
mustBeRight.detail: A flat band of the `ice` ramp below the gates with a lit top edge and a couple of straight sheen bars. NO spray, NO foam, NO falling water, NO boat.

simplifyAway: the chains, the crab winches, the gate paddles and the hinge ironwork
individual stones: five courses and a handful of joints are the whole masonry
the second and third chambers of the flight: one chamber is the subject
the buildings above the lock in the reference photograph, including the large hotel that dominates it
neverAdd: a boat, a canoe, a barge or a lock-keeper
falling water, spray, foam or a waterfall: the reference is a summer exposure with the gates spilling and this level is winter
a name, a number, a plaque, an interpretive panel or any lettering in either language
a flag or a flagpole (OQ-ART-04 is open)
a swing bridge, a footbridge or a road over the chamber: the level already draws one bridge, on layer-50-canalwall
notes: ottawa/rideau-canal-ottawa-locks.jpg is the only reference and it is a SUMMER exposure taken from
below, looking up: the gates are spilling, the sky is bright and the hotel above fills the top two
thirds of the frame. What it settles is the MECHANISM and the masonry - the mitre, the beams, the
coursing, the handrail - and nothing about the season. The winter is the level's, and the snow and
the ice come from palette.json.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none is set; a lock at 120 px is still a pair of gates. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an
identification: at 180 px wide the mitre seam, both balance beams, both handrails and four of the
five courses survive. The 120 px silhouette is the weakest of this level's four heroes - a lock is
mostly negative space - and it still reads as two walls with a low structure between them.

expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT MAY BE ASKED FOR A BUILDING AND MUST NOT BE ASKED FOR A CITY. It is a single
non-repeating POI hero of one specific building whose stack - a sixteen-sided sandstone drum ringed
with buttresses and pinnacles, three tall pointed windows, a deep cornice, and a very steep ribbed
polygonal roof with a ring of gabled dormers under a small stone lantern - is not shared by anything
else this game will draw. But the level already has an anchor that carries Ottawa, `parliament-hill`,
and this one is deliberately not asked to do it twice.
THE FAILURE TO WATCH FOR IS "a church", "a chapel" or "a cathedral chapter house". The roof, the
pointed windows and the pinnacles are all genuinely ecclesiastical in origin - that is what Gothic
Revival is - and the things that keep it a library are the absence of a cross, of a bell stage and
of a west door, and the presence of a plain spike finial. An identification of "a chapter house" is
accepted above because the building IS one architecturally; "a church" is not.

mustBeRight.feature: a very steep polygonal roof with radiating ribs, much taller than the wall under it
mustBeRight.why: It is three quarters of the silhouette and it is the single thing that identifies the building at any size.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on ottawa/parliament-hill-north-library.jpg, in the column through the building's axis: the roof is about 430 px tall over a 490 px base, so HEIGHT : BASE = 0.88. The shipped art draws 360 over 480 = 0.75 with the lantern above it, and the whole roof assembly including the lantern 410 over 480 = 0.85. Anything under about 0.6 stops being this building and becomes a bandstand. Seven or eight ribs run from the apex to the eave in a lighter tone; they are the facets of the polygon, not decoration.

mustBeRight.feature: a ring of small gabled dormers with pointed-arch heads around the lower third of the roof
mustBeRight.detail: Five visible, evenly spaced, the middle one a little higher than its neighbours, each a small stone gable with a pointed opening. Rhythm, not count: the real building has sixteen and the number may differ, the shape and the spacing-to-width ratio may not.

mustBeRight.feature: a polygonal sandstone drum ringed by stepped buttresses that rise into pinnacles
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes the building round rather than square, and the buttresses are what carry the eye from the wall into the roof.
mustBeRight.detail: Four visible buttresses standing proud of the wall, each capped by a pointed pinnacle that rises above the eave line and in front of the roof. Buff sandstone - the `stone` ramp, which is Nepean sandstone and is what Parliament Hill is built of - and NOT brick and NOT limestone.

mustBeRight.feature: three tall pointed-arch windows between the buttresses, dark against the stone
mustBeRight.detail: Two thirds the height of the wall, each with one mullion and one transom. Glazing bars beyond that cross are simplified away, the same substitution the Peace Tower made on its dial.

mustBeRight.feature: a small stone lantern with a dark cap and a plain spike finial at the apex
mustBeRight.detail: A short polygonal drum sitting ON the roof apex, a small dark cone over it, then a plain spike and a ball. The reference carries a crocketed iron finial with a weathervane; it becomes a spike and a ball.

mustBeRight.feature: snow on every upward surface, and the ground it stands on is snow
mustBeRight.detail: On the dormer gables, on the pinnacle caps, on the cornice, and a swept snow bank at the foot. This level is winter; the file's bottom edge IS the level ground line and `theme.ground` is snow-base.

simplifyAway: the flying buttresses of the real building: they become stepped wall buttresses, which is what reads at this size
the carved crockets, finials and gargoyles
the iron cresting along the eave
the Centre Block, the Peace Tower and everything else in the reference photograph: this hero is the library alone, and the Peace Tower is another subject
the shingle courses of the roof: the ribs are the whole roof structure
neverAdd: a cross, a crucifix, a bell, a belfry stage or any religious emblem. This is the single most likely wrong addition to a steep-roofed polygonal Gothic building and it would turn a library into a church

a clock face. Scoped deliberately: a clock is REQUIRED of peace-tower and forbidden here, and the reason is that the two subjects are judged in the same hand-off and this level must not have two clock towers
a flag or a flagpole (OQ-ART-04 is open)
a statue, a bust or a carved figure
any lettering, inscription, date stone or wordmark in either language

a green copper roof. Scoped deliberately: copper green is REQUIRED of parliament-hill and forbidden here. The library's roof reads dark in every reference in this repository, and drawing it green would merge the two subjects at phone size
notes: ottawa/parliament-hill-north-library.jpg is the PRIMARY reference: the library from the north with
the Peace Tower and Centre Block beside it. It is a DARK OVERCAST exposure - the sky is a grey field
and the stone reads brown-black - so it is a GEOMETRY reference only and every colour comes from
palette.json. The ratios above were read off a 200 x 280 crop of it, enlarged; that is the honest
limit of a 960 x 720 photograph in which the building is 200 px wide, and no finer figure is claimed.
THE HERO ALREADY CONTAINS THIS BUILDING, AND THAT IS STATED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE FOUND.
landmark-parliament-hill@1x.svg draws the library as a SPIRE TIP behind the right wing - a dark cone and
a finial, about 60 px wide, with no drum, no dormers, no buttresses and no windows. This subject is the
building itself at ten times that area. A verifier who sees both should read them as the far view and
the near view of one building, which is what they are; they are 1800 px apart in the level because a
side-scrolling level lays its subjects along a line, the same abstraction that puts the Halifax Town
Clock and Pier 21 3400 px apart when they are three kilometres apart in life.
WHY THIS BUILDING IS THE SECOND PARLIAMENT SUBJECT. The level's hero, parliament-hill, is the Peace
Tower and Centre Block. The library is the only part of the original building that survived the 1916
fire, which is the fact its POI blurb carries, and it is the one other piece of that group whose
shape is unmistakable on its own.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw it below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise it,
adopted from the Ottawa floor rather than re-derived. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at
180 px wide the ribs, all five dormers, the lantern, the three windows and the four pinnacles
survive; the 120 px silhouette is a steep ribbed cone on a ringed drum with a lantern on top.

subjects.subject: A warming hut standing on canal ice
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswer: a shelter on a frozen lake or canal
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. It is a hut, and the real ones carry an operator's wordmark and livery, neither
of which this project draws. No answer here names a city or a canal and the gate must not reward one.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY IS THAT IT STANDS ON ICE. "A house", "a shed" or "a cabin in the woods" without
the ice is a partial answer; the scored ice band under it and the skate marks are what place it.

mustBeRight.feature: a low, long timber cabin under a shallow gable roof carrying snow
mustBeRight.why: Low and long is the whole proportion. A tall hut with a steep roof is an alpine chalet and belongs to a different country.
mustBeRight.detail: The wall is about three times as wide as it is tall and the roof pitch is shallow - roughly one in six - with a deep snow load along it and a lit edge on the near slope.

mustBeRight.feature: two lit windows and one dark open doorway
mustBeRight.why: Lit windows are what say WARM, which is the entire purpose of the building and the reason a player would walk to it.
mustBeRight.detail: Windows in a warm light tone inside a white frame; the doorway a flat dark opening with a white frame and no door leaf drawn. The lit tone is `brass-light`, which no other element on this level uses.

mustBeRight.feature: painted panels on the boarding, in a red that is not the flag red
mustBeRight.detail: Two panels flanking the door, in the `oxide` ramp. The huts in the reference are dark boarding with red panels; `oxide` is the same red the Peggy's Cove fish stores use and is deliberately not `flag-red`, because OQ-ART-04 is open and nothing in this game asserts the flag's red.

mustBeRight.feature: ice at its foot, scored by skates, and no snow bank
mustBeRight.why: A snow bank would put the hut on the shore. It stands on the frozen canal, which is what the level's locomotion is about.
mustBeRight.detail: A flat band of the `ice` ramp across the bottom of the file with a lit top edge and three or four straight sheen bars for skate scoring. The file's bottom edge IS the level ground line, which on this stretch is world y 1468, on the ice.

mustBeRight.feature: a plank bench along the wall
mustBeRight.detail: Where skates are put on, and the one piece of furniture that explains the building. Two legs, a plank seat, a lit top edge.

simplifyAway: the operator's signage, wordmarks, banners and pricing boards, which is most of what is on the real hut
the stovepipe, the cables and the fittings below 12 px
the crowd around it: this hero draws no figure at all
the boarding pattern of the walls: art-bible section 1 forbids a surface pattern
neverAdd: any lettering, wordmark, logo or price in either language
a national flag or a maple leaf device (OQ-ART-04 is open)
a figure, on the ice or in the doorway
hockey boards, nets or line markings: the skateway is not a rink
a chimney with smoke drawn as a plume: smoke is a filter effect in cartoon shorthand and ADR-0011 wants every effect to have a plain path
notes: ottawa/rideau-canal-skateway-portrait.jpg is the primary reference: the change hut on the ice with
skaters in front of it and the bridge beyond. It is a bright winter exposure and the colours are
usable, but the building in it is heavily branded and the drawing takes only the FORM.
THIS LEVEL ALREADY HAS A HUT, and it is not this one. layer-50-canalwall.svg carries a small warming
hut on the FAR retaining wall, across the canal, as part of a tile that repeats every 2016 px. This
hero stands on the near ice beside the player, at one world x, at four times the size. The
relationship is the same as peggys-cove's seven far fish stores and its one near fish-store hero,
and it is recorded here so a verifier who sees both does not report a duplication.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px the two lit windows,
the doorway, the red panels, the snow load, the bench and the spruce all survive; the 120 px
silhouette is a long low gabled box with a small conifer beside it.

subjects.subject: A Canadian police constable in ceremonial scarlet review order (the 'Mountie' silhouette)
expectedBlindAnswer: Canadian police officer in red dress uniform

mustBeRight.feature: scarlet tunic
mustBeRight.detail: Single-breasted, high standing collar, fitted to the waist then flaring into a short skirt below the belt. Two breast pockets with pointed, scalloped flaps.

mustBeRight.feature: dark collar and shoulder straps
mustBeRight.why: The colour break at the collar and shoulders is what stops the tunic reading as a plain red coat.
mustBeRight.detail: Midnight blue, distinctly darker than the tunic.

mustBeRight.feature: wide-brimmed felt hat
mustBeRight.why: The strongest silhouette read at small size.
mustBeRight.detail: Tan felt, flat level brim about 1.4 head-widths across, crown pinched to a point with a fore-and-aft crease, brown leather band with a small buckle.
mustBeRight.maskRegionNote: The hat window in character space, which is the space the single-figure render is built in. DIAGNOSTIC, never gating: it answers how much of the identification the brim alone carries, which is the question the first hand pass could not ask. officer.md 2 claims the brim is the single strongest read at small size; this is how that claim gets tested rather than asserted. NOTHING IN THIS RIG MAY SIT ABOVE y = 0: the composite crops negative origins, so a crown that overhangs the canvas is handed to the identifier with a flat top, and a maskRegion quoting such a frame verbatim makes the hand-off refuse to build. Both were true of the hat for one afternoon.

mustBeRight.feature: brown leather belt with a diagonal cross-strap
mustBeRight.why: The diagonal is half the identity of a Sam Browne. A plain waist belt loses it.
mustBeRight.detail: Wide waist belt with a brass buckle, and one strap from the wearer's right shoulder down to the left hip.

mustBeRight.feature: dark breeches with a yellow-gold stripe down the outer seam
mustBeRight.why: Does more identification work than its area suggests. If it disappears first at small size, thicken it.
mustBeRight.detail: Midnight blue, full at the thigh and close below the knee, one broad stripe running the full leg.
mustBeRight.whyMasked: MEASURED against the 240x470 composite the renderRecipe builds: this rectangle covers both thighs and both gold stripes and leaves the tunic, hat, gloves and boots untouched. It exists because assets/style/officer.md asserts the stripe 'does more identification work than its area suggests' and 'if it disappears first at small size, thicken it' - a testable claim that until now had no test. One rectangle covers both stripes only because it covers the breeches too, which is correct: the FEATURE is the breeches-with-stripe, not the stripe alone.

mustBeRight.feature: high brown riding boots
mustBeRight.detail: To just below the knee, with a strap and buckle at the ankle. Breeches tuck in.

mustBeRight.feature: brass buttons in a single centre row
mustBeRight.detail: Read as a rhythm of round brass dots, not as modelled buttons.

mustBeRight.feature: the figure is TURNED TOWARD THE DIRECTION IT TRAVELS
mustBeRight.why: This is a portrait 2D side-scroller and every character in it walks, skates, toboggans or bikes ALONG the screen. A character drawn front-on, facing the viewer, is wrong by construction - it reads as a menu portrait somebody slid sideways - and that is what the repository owner reported from the live site: that it is looking at the user. A verifier who describes the figure as facing the camera, or who cannot say which way it is going, FAILS this entry. Nothing in this file asked about it before 2026-09-09, which is why a front-on side-scroller character shipped. JUDGE IT AT 390 px, NOT AT 1x. The first correction turned the body and left the head at the body angle; it passed every 1x render it was shown in, and at phone width the guide read as travelling while both humans read as standing still looking at the player. A cue that is 2 px on a phone is not a cue.
mustBeRight.detail: Three-quarter, canonical facing RIGHT. The BODY sits about 40 degrees off strict profile and the HEAD is turned to the same three-quarter, with the whole face - both eyes and the mouth - on its leading half, which keeps the chest plane the officer cross-strap needs. Redrawn 2026-09-14 (art-bible.md 7.7): the head used to be turned further, to about 25 degrees off profile, with the face crowded onto its front edge, and at phone size that read as a snout. WHAT CARRIES IT AT PHONE SIZE IS THE HEAD OUTLINE: an asymmetric silhouette with a big round cranium behind, one ear set back, and the jaw and a small rounded nose on the leading edge, the nose projecting about 7 px past the cheek line. Supporting cues, in the order they survive being made small: the hair mass at the BACK with the fringe sweeping forward; the chest plane and its fastening on the leading edge; BOTH feet pointing the way the character travels; the neck, a lit column between jaw and a darker collar, without which the head-and-shoulder mass reads as one lump; the hat brim swung forward, or the toque band running STEEPLY downhill to the back - level over the face, because it must clear the brows, and dropping behind it; both eyes on the front half of the face, well clear of the outline, the far one foreshortened; and ONE ear, well back. The near side is the wearer right side, so the near arm and leg draw in front. See art-bible.md 7.1.

mustBeRight.feature: cartoon proportions identical to every other character
mustBeRight.why: CLAUDE.md requires it and docs/content-review.md 6.2 gives the reason: comparison only works if everyone is compared. A verifier shown ONE figure cannot check this and must not be asked to, so the hand-off carries a second figure on the same rig in a different costume. TIGHTENED 2026-09-09 after the repository owner reported the player shoulders as out of proportion and THIS ENTRY HAD SCORED PRESENT ANYWAY. It scored present because it asked only whether two figures matched, and they did - they were equally wrong, both built to a canon whose shoulder row was 54 percent over a measured photograph. An entry that cannot see the widest part of a figure is not measuring proportions, so it now names that measurement, gives the number, gives the reference the number came from, and says which quantity is allowed to differ.
mustBeRight.detail: 6 heads tall, 420 px crown to sole at design resolution, head 70 px. MEASURE THE WIDEST POINT OF EACH FIGURE - not the shoulder line by eye, the widest point, wherever it falls - as a fraction of that figure own crown-to-sole height. AND CHECK THE NECK: every figure must show a column of its own surface between the jaw and the collar, 12 to 13 px at design resolution, about 4 px at 390 px, with the collar DARKER than the column beneath it. A figure whose head sits straight on the shoulders FAILS this entry however well its width measures - that was reported from the live site as "the head is on the torso" and it is most of why the shoulders still looked wrong after their width was corrected. It is derived, not chosen: 0.149 of head height, measured on officer/red-serge-full-figure.jpg, see art-bible.md 7.3. The guide is held to the same column in pelt rather than skin, which is a surface exemption for one non-human artboard and not a licence to draw it neckless. On the shipped art that is 115 px, at the skirt with the gloves hanging beside it, on a 430 px figure, which is 0.267 of its own height; the hat brim is 106 px and is headgear above the crown, measured beside the body and not as part of it, exactly as the player toque is. The cap for every character is 116 px, which is 0.276 of height. It is derived, not chosen: an adult in a winter parka in assets/refs/ottawa/rideau-canal-skateway-ice.jpg measures 0.238 of their own height across the shoulders with the arms hanging in, and 0.276 is that plus a deliberate cartoon broadening of about a tenth. A figure at or over 0.30 FAILS this entry however well it matches the figure beside it.
mustBeRight.whatMayDiffer: THE GARMENT, WITHIN THE CAP. A parka genuinely broadens the shoulders and a fitted tunic barely does, so the three costumes measure the serge 115, the parka 115 and the beaver 116 px at rest, arms included. A verifier should NOT fail the pair over a few pixels of coat.
mustBeRight.whatMayNotDiffer: THE FIGURE. Crown line, sole line, eye line, the heights of the shoulder, hip, knee and ankle, the size of the hands and of the feet, the head size and the three stroke weights are IDENTICAL between the officer and the player and the guide, because they are the same rig and, for the limbs and hands, literally the same atlas frames. If a verifier can see that one figure head is bigger, its eye line higher or its hands larger, that is the failure this entry is for.

It scored present because it asked only whether two figures matched, and they did - they were equally wrong, both built to a canon whose shoulder row was 54 percent over a measured photograph. An entry that cannot see the widest part of a figure is not measuring proportions, so it now names that measurement, gives the number, gives the reference the number came from, and says which quantity is allowed to differ.
mustBeRight.detail: 6 heads tall, 420 px crown to sole at design resolution, head 70 px. MEASURE THE WIDEST POINT OF EACH FIGURE - not the shoulder line by eye, the widest point, wherever it falls - as a fraction of that figure own crown-to-sole height. AND CHECK THE NECK: every figure must show a column of its own surface between the jaw and the collar, 12 to 13 px at design resolution, about 4 px at 390 px, with the collar DARKER than the column beneath it. A figure whose head sits straight on the shoulders FAILS this entry however well its width measures - that was reported from the live site as "the head is on the torso" and it is most of why the shoulders still looked wrong after their width was corrected. It is derived, not chosen: 0.149 of head height, measured on officer/red-serge-full-figure.jpg, see art-bible.md 7.3. The guide is held to the same column in pelt rather than skin, which is a surface exemption for one non-human artboard and not a licence to draw it neckless. On the shipped art that is 115 px, at the hem with the mitts hanging beside it, on a 430 px figure, which is 0.267 of its own height. The cap for every character is 116 px, which is 0.276 of height. It is derived, not chosen: an adult in a winter parka in assets/refs/ottawa/rideau-canal-skateway-ice.jpg measures 0.238 of their own height across the shoulders with the arms hanging in, and 0.276 is that plus a deliberate cartoon broadening of about a tenth. A figure at or over 0.30 FAILS this entry however well it matches the figure beside it.
mustBeRight.whatMayDiffer: THE GARMENT, WITHIN THE CAP. A parka genuinely broadens the shoulders and a fitted tunic barely does, so the three costumes measure the parka 115, the serge 115 and the beaver 116 px at rest, arms included. A verifier should NOT fail the pair over a few pixels of coat.
mustBeRight.whatMayNotDiffer: THE FIGURE. Crown line, sole line, eye line, the heights of the shoulder, hip, knee and ankle, the size of the hands and of the feet, the head size and the three stroke weights are IDENTICAL between the player and the officer and the guide, because they are the same rig and, for the limbs and hands, literally the same atlas frames. If a verifier can see that one figure head is bigger, its eye line higher or its hands larger, that is the failure this entry is for.

simplifyAway: fabric folds and drape
stitching, seam topstitching and zip teeth
laces above the boot cuff
fur strand detail on the hood trim
separated fingers, at any size
neverAdd: a national flag, a maple leaf or any emblem on the costume
lettering of any kind, in any language, anywhere on the character
a diagonal band, strap or sash running shoulder to hip - that is the officer's Sam Browne
a red coat or tunic - the officer is scarlet and the two must not converge at small size
any insignia, badge, crest or rank marking
a facial feature that identifies an ethnicity once colour is removed (docs/content-review.md 6.3)
subjects.whyTheOmissions: The Canadian read is carried by the kit - parka, toque, scarf, mitts, snow boots - and not by an emblem. An emblem on the player is also a decoration the player did not choose, on a character whose entire point is that the player chose it.
notes: referenceFiles is empty and that stays correct: this is a costume, not a landmark, and there is no photograph it is a simplification OF. The accuracy bar it has to clear is the palette, the proportion canon and the two-size test. ONE OF THOSE THREE IS NOW MEASURED FROM A PHOTOGRAPH ANYWAY, and it is named here rather than added above, because it is a reference for the FIGURE and not for the costume: assets/refs/ottawa/rideau-canal-skateway-ice.jpg (CC0-1.0, already credited) carries an adult in a winter parka, full length, facing the camera, and the shoulder rows in art-bible.md 7.2 are measured off them. Before that measurement the canon said 154 px of shoulder on a 420 px figure and nobody could say where the number came from, which is how it survived being 54 percent wrong.

The blind answer does not have to contain the word Canadian. Parka, toque, scarf and mitts on a 6-head cartoon figure is the target; a verifier who says 'a person dressed for cold weather' has passed.

subjects.subject: The Chateau Frontenac, Quebec City
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `singleSource()`, the same builder as peace-tower.
expectedBlindAnswer: the castle hotel in Quebec City
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THE KIND OF THING PASSES; THE PLACE NAME IS A BONUS. Amended 2026-09-17: a blind viewer cannot read
a proper noun off a drawing that carries no lettering, so `a castle hotel` now PASSES and the
proper names stay accepted as strong positive evidence. What follows is why this subject MAY carry a
place name at all, which is still true and is still the difference from the toboggan run below.
This subject is ALLOWED to be asked for a place name, unlike the toboggan-run subject below, and the difference
is not a preference: this render is a single non-repeating POI hero that draws one specific building, so a
verifier who cannot tell it is a castle-like grand hotel is reporting a defect in the drawing, and one who
sees that and cannot put a city to it is reporting the limit of what a drawing can say. The toboggan run is two repeating parallax
tiles that may not carry a landmark at all, so a verifier who names Quebec City from THEM would be reporting
a defect too - in the opposite direction. Ottawa learned that the hard way: its canal contract demanded
"Ottawa" from a tile its own notes forbade putting an Ottawa cue on, and it passed on the verifier's
inference rather than on the art.

mustBeRight.feature: green copper roofs over red-brown brick walls
mustBeRight.why: The single strongest cue and the one a newcomer carries in their head. Green roofs on red-brown brick is the Chateau Frontenac and very little else in Canada. It is also the pair that separates this landmark from Ottawa's: Parliament Hill is green copper over PALE BUFF SANDSTONE, and if both landmarks are drawn in the same stone the game has two buildings that look like each other.
mustBeRight.detail: Use the `copper` ramp for the wing and turret roofs and the `brick` ramp for the walls. `brick` was added to palette.json for this landmark, base hsl(18,52%,44%): MEASURED 2026-09-08 as the hue-filtered median of 106441 sunlit wall pixels in chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg, #a27447 = hsl(29,42%,46%) under low warm autumn sun, against #735749 = hsl(20,21%,37%) for the same wall under overcast winter light in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg. The base sits between them and more saturated, per art-bible section 2. Pale stone banding runs horizontally across the brick; use `stone-light`. NOT grey, NOT sandstone buff for the walls.

mustBeRight.feature: very steep roofs, 60 degrees or more from horizontal
mustBeRight.why: The defining property of the chateau style and the thing that is lost first when a cartoon flattens a roof. A 30 degree roof on this massing is a Victorian hotel, not a chateau, and no amount of green brings it back.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED from the roof silhouette by sky segmentation rather than by eye: the central tower's roof slope is 64.5 and 64.4 degrees on the two sides in chateau-frontenac-dusk.jpg (left slope (600,244)->(660,118), right slope (960,139)->(1030,285)), 62.7 degrees in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg, and 60.2 degrees in chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg ((890,376)->(945,280)). The shipped art draws every roof end, gable and lucarne at 62 degrees and the tower roof at 62.3. Anything under 45 degrees stops being a chateau roof.

mustBeRight.feature: one dominant square tower with a pyramidal roof, rising from the centre of a long mass
mustBeRight.why: The composition. Without the tower this reads as a generic Victorian railway hotel - which is what the maskRegion below exists to test, and it is the most useful single thing anyone can measure about this subject.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg (1124x1600), the long-lens near-orthographic elevation, which is the ONE internally consistent view of the three and is therefore the one the drawing is built to. Tower width 161.7 px; total height base(620) to crest(91.7) = 528.3, so WIDTH : HEIGHT = 1 : 3.27. Wing ridge at y=380, so wing height 240 and TOWER : WING = 2.20. Tower standing above the wing ridge = 288.3, which is 0.55 of the total and 1.78 of the tower's width. The other two views bracket these: chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg gives 1:2.85 and 1.84 (oblique, so the tower's width is inflated by seeing two faces), chateau-frontenac-dusk.jpg gives 2.30 (close, from below, base hidden behind the wings, so its width:height of 1:1.40 is DISCARDED rather than averaged). The shipped art is 220 x 720 = 1 : 3.27, tower:wing 2.20, 0.55 above the ridge, 1.79 of the width above it. Anything squatter than 1 : 2.5 stops being this tower.
mustBeRight.whyMasked: MEASURED against the shipped 1080x900 render: this rectangle covers the tower's finial, its pyramidal roof, the roof's eaves board and the shaft down to the wing ridge at world y 773 (render row 473), and leaves both wings, all four turret cones, every green roof, the brick, the banding, the arcade and the rock untouched. Verified by compositing the mask and looking. DIAGNOSTIC, never gating: it exists to put a number on the claim that the tower is what makes this the Chateau Frontenac rather than a chateau-style hotel, which is otherwise an assertion nobody can check.

mustBeRight.feature: the tower roof is markedly darker than the wing roofs
mustBeRight.why: It is true in every reference here and it is what stops the building reading as one flat green mass. Drawing the tower roof green as well loses the tonal hierarchy that makes the tower dominant.
mustBeRight.detail: The wings and turret cones are green copper; the central tower's roof is a dark slate-grey-green in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg, chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg, chateau-frontenac-tower-2024.jpg and chateau-frontenac-dusk.jpg alike. The shipped art uses the `slate` ramp for it against `copper` for the wings.

mustBeRight.feature: conical turrets, several of them, in a rhythm along the mass
mustBeRight.why: The turret count is what makes the building read as a chateau at small size; when everything else has collapsed, the cone silhouette is still there.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED apex angles: 33-36 degrees for the tall corner turrets in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg (three turrets on the right wing at crop x 920-970, 1020-1090 and 1140-1200), and up to 50 degrees for the smaller ones in chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg. The shipped art draws every cone at a 40 degree apex, inside that band. RHYTHM, NOT COUNT (art-bible rule 3): the number of turrets may differ from the photograph; the apex angle and the spacing may not. A cone wider than a 60 degree apex reads as a circus tent and is wrong.

mustBeRight.feature: gabled dormers in a rhythm along the green roofs
mustBeRight.why: It is what stops the long roofs reading as plain green wedges, and it is present in every reference.
mustBeRight.detail: Lucarnes with their own steep gables at the same pitch as the roof, breaking the ridge line, with a small finial. Spacing to width about 1.6, measured on the long wing in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg (seven dormers at about 45 crop px spacing on 28 crop px width). The number may differ from the photograph; the ratio may not.

mustBeRight.feature: the building stands on rock, above a terrace, not on flat ground
mustBeRight.why: Half of what the photographs show is that this building is on a cliff. Cap Diamant is why the Chateau is where it is, and a chateau on flat ground is a hotel.
mustBeRight.detail: A rock mass in vertical facets under the terrace level, with snow lying on its ledges and a few spruces at its foot. chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg shows the terrace's buttressed retaining wall dropping away below the building; dufferin-terrace-toboggan-slide-1905.jpg shows the same drop from the other side.

simplifyAway: brick coursing and mortar joints
window mullions, transoms and glazing bars
the individual facets of the polygonal turret roofs: four facets read as a cone, sixteen read as noise
balcony ironwork and fire escapes
roof vents, aerials, satellite dishes and the rooftop plant enclosure that sits on the tower's flat deck
the hotel's own signage, awnings and flags: nothing in this level draws lettering of any kind

the corbelled corner bartizans on the tower shaft. DROPPED, NOT APPROXIMATED, and it took three attempts to admit it: at 220 px of tower width a bartizan is a 46 px drum under a 27 px cone and it reads as a brown lozenge stuck to the tower. Art-bible rule 4 is drop, never substitute. The stone quoin strips at the tower's corners, which are also really there, stay and do the job.
neverAdd: a clock face anywhere on this building. There is no clock on the Chateau Frontenac, and a cartoon tower tempts an artist into one; drawing it would also make this landmark and Ottawa's the same landmark
battlements, crenellation or arrow slits: this is an 1893 railway hotel in chateau style, not a fortress, and the difference is the whole point of the roofs
a dome, a minaret, or a second dominant tower
a drawbridge, a portcullis or a moat
the fleur-de-lys or any flag, coat of arms, wordmark or emblem: the game draws no lettering and no heraldry, and a flag on this building would assert something the art has not verified
snow lying in a sheet on the roof planes. At 62 degrees these roofs shed, and every winter reference here shows them clear; snow lies on the ledges, the dormer heads, the cornices and the ground
notes: chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg is the PRIMARY reference and the only one whose ratios are internally
consistent. Measure against it; use the others to bracket and to sanity-check.
chateau-frontenac-tower-2024.jpg carries no colour profile and its white balance is markedly cool - a
hue-filtered median over its whole facade returns ZERO brick-hued pixels. Use it for geometry only. It is
the same trap as Ottawa's night clock photograph, in a different disguise.
chateau-frontenac-dusk.jpg is a dusk exposure with the building floodlit and coloured architectural lighting
on the tower. Use it for massing and for the roof-slope measurement, never for colour.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw this landmark below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise it.
That is the verifier's floor from Ottawa, adopted here rather than re-derived, because no blind pass has been
run on this subject yet. What the size ladder shows as a DRAWING OBSERVATION, which is not an identification:
at 300 px every mustBeRight feature is legible including the lucarne rhythm; at 140 px the lucarnes, the stone
banding and the windows have collapsed to speckle and the read rests entirely on the four cone silhouettes,
the dark central pyramid and the green-on-red contrast. Whether that is still enough is the identifier's call,
not the artist's, and the floor stays at 300 until someone makes it.
The two-size test in art-bible section 5 was run at the shipping size of 1080 x 900 and passed at both probes.
That is what ADR-0013 as amended requires before a landmark ships at 1x rather than the 2x default; the
measured saving is 14.83 MiB -> 3.71 MiB of decoded texture. See assets/style/quebec-city-level.md section 5.

subjects.subject: A toboggan run beside a railed winter promenade
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, terrace above run, the run placed 580 px below the terrace tile's top edge (world y 1280 against 700). Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x=0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (2016 and 1440) rather than laying them side by side, and draw the run over the terrace where they overlap, which is the order the level uses. Neither file answers the subject alone: a run with no promenade is a snowy field, and a promenade with no run is a fence. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'terrace', nearMatch: 'slope', nearTop: 580 })`, the same shape and the same offset as the Rideau Canal.
expectedBlindAnswer: a boardwalk and a snow chute
a railed promenade and a snow run
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE, and this list is the whole reason this note exists. Both renders are REPEATING parallax
tiles - 2016 px and 1440 px - so a unique landmark drawn on either appears three or four times across the
level. Nothing on them may name a city, and it follows that nothing may be DEMANDED of them that names one.
Ottawa's canal subject asked its verifier for "Ottawa" from a tile whose own notes forbade drawing the one
landmark that would have said Ottawa; it passed on the verifier's inference from project context rather than
on the art, and had to be amended. That mistake is not repeated here: no answer in this list names Quebec
City, Quebec, the Dufferin Terrace or the Chateau Frontenac, and a verifier who does name one of them is not
wrong - they are just not required to, and the gate must not reward it.
WHERE QUEBEC CITY ACTUALLY COMES FROM: the level composite. `quebec-city-landmark-chateau-frontenac` is a
separate, non-repeating subject that draws one specific building and IS required to be named. The run is where
the player toboggans; the Chateau is what says which city. Splitting them is what lets each be judged on what
it actually contains.

Every answer here is deliberately free of ordinary connectives four letters or longer. "a boardwalk with an ornate railing above a snow slope" was in this list for one run and failed the hand-off's leak scan on the token "with". See the note on quebec-city-riverfront.

mustBeRight.feature: the snow lane is a built chute with edges, not open hillside
mustBeRight.why: This is a toboggan RUN, not a snowy field. The containment is the whole read, exactly as the built edges are what make Ottawa's ice a canal rather than a pond.
mustBeRight.detail: Both references show a chute with high walls and long straight lane dividers running downhill. TrueNorth is a portrait side-scroller and looks ACROSS the run, where the view down it does not exist, so in the side view the containment reads as: a low timber wall running the full width along the far side of the lane with snow capping it, two straight level lane-divider ridges running the full width, and a near snow bank framing the bottom of the frame. Straight, level, parallel edges - a built chute, never a natural slope. AMENDED 2026-09-08 after a genuinely blind pass recorded this feature ABSENT and read the whole lower half as a frozen ice-covered river: the two lane dividers were a boundary between two flat colour bands, which reads as a change of surface, not as a raised ridge. Each divider is now MODELLED - a shaded far flank, a lit crest and a shaded near flank - so it reads as a bank of snow standing above the lane.

mustBeRight.feature: straight parallel runner marks in the lane
mustBeRight.why: A toboggan runner scores STRAIGHT lines. The curved arcs that are correct on skated ice would say skating rink, which is a different level of this game and a different sport.
mustBeRight.detail: Sparse, straight, level, parallel streaks in `snow-light` at 0.30-0.42 opacity, authored as shapes. Never noise, never arcs.

mustBeRight.feature: a promenade above the run with an ornate cast-iron railing
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes the run a town amenity rather than a hillside, and the scroll-panel railing is the strongest single piece of built character on these tiles.
mustBeRight.detail: A masonry parapet with a snow-capped coping, and along its head a dark green cast-iron railing of repeating scroll panels between posts with urn finials, drawn from dufferin-terrace-boardwalk.jpg. Two arcs and a ring per bay - rhythm, not tracery.

mustBeRight.feature: globe lamp standards in a rhythm along the promenade
mustBeRight.why: Present in both terrace references and in the 1905 photograph; it is what dates and places the promenade without naming it.
mustBeRight.detail: Dark green columns with a cluster of three white opal globes, one central and two on curved brackets.

mustBeRight.feature: people in winter coats, standing and walking, not skating or skiing
mustBeRight.why: CLAUDE.md requires identical cartoon proportions for every character, and background figures are where that rule is quietly broken first.
mustBeRight.detail: Six heads tall, the same proportion canon as the player, drawn small because they are further away and never because they matter less. Winter coats, toques, mitts, boots. No outline: a figure authored into a parallax tile is background. NO CULTURAL MARKER OF ANY KIND on any of them - docs/content-review.md 3.3 outcome 2, and it is a rule here rather than an oversight.

mustBeRight.feature: the lane is PACKED SNOW, and never the `ice` ramp
mustBeRight.why: AMENDED 2026-09-08, and this is the most useful thing anyone has learned about this subject. This entry used to say "use the `ice` ramp for the polished lane against `snow` for the banks", which made the lane the same blue-white ramp as the Rideau Canal Skateway - IN THE SAME HAND-OFF. A blind verifier read the render as a frozen river with wind-blown ice streaks and scored the built-chute feature absent; none of the eight accepted answers is about water, so the subject was not read as a toboggan run at all. Feature 6 was fighting feature 1 and the strongest colour signal won. Correctly drawn runner marks cannot outvote a ramp.
mustBeRight.detail: Use the `snow` ramp for the lane: `snow-base` for the lane body, `snow-light` for the sunlit crests and near lip, `snow-shade` for the flanks and the scored grooves. The `ice` ramp belongs to the Rideau Canal and must not appear anywhere on this lane.

mustBeRight.feature: at least one rider seated on a flat wooden toboggan, on the lane
mustBeRight.why: ADDED 2026-09-08. There was no toboggan and no rider anywhere in 2016 px of this composite, and a blind verifier is being asked to name a sport from an empty surface. The single cheapest thing that says toboggan run is a toboggan on it.
mustBeRight.detail: Seated, knees up, leaning back, one hand on the rope, on a flat wooden deck with a curled front - the posture in quebec-city/toboggan-slide-riders.jpg. Six heads tall in the standing canon, drawn seated. No outline: a figure authored into a parallax tile is background. No cultural marker of any kind.

simplifyAway: individual planks in the boardwalk decking
the cast-iron railing's real tracery: two arcs and a ring per bay is the rhythm, and the rest is below 12 px
street furniture above the lamp line
faces on the background figures below 12 px
neverAdd: the Chateau Frontenac, or any other named or recognisable building, drawn into either of these two REPEATING tiles. Scoped deliberately: the Chateau is required on the chateau-frontenac subject and forbidden here, and the reason is the tiling, not the building. A prohibition on one subject may not forbid a requirement of another (verifyArtProtocol.contradictionRule), so this one names the tiles it applies to
hockey boards, nets or line markings: this is a slide, not a rink
a ski lift, a chairlift or a tow rope
mountains on the horizon
any lettering, signage or wordmark, in either language

the `ice` ramp anywhere on the lane. Scoped deliberately: `ice` is required of rideau-canal-skateway and forbidden here, and the reason is that the two subjects are judged in the same hand-off and a shared ramp made one of them read as the other

a recognisable building of any kind on these repeating tiles, INCLUDING street furniture. The terrace tile carried a striped bandstand kiosk with a green-and-white radial roof and a white finial, drawn from quebec-city/dufferin-terrace-boardwalk.jpg, and an unprimed verifier named Terrasse Dufferin, Quebec City off it - from a tile whose own rule this list already was. It is now a plain open timber shelter. The lesson generalises: furniture that is really architecture is architecture
notes: dufferin-terrace-toboggan-slide-1905.jpg is the level's composition reference: the chute, its walls, the
promenade beside it and the crowd, in one frame. toboggan-slide-riders.jpg gives the riders' posture -
seated, knees up, leaning back on a flat wooden toboggan - and the lane structure.
Both historical photographs show timber hoop arches over the run. The shipped tile draws ONE timber
footbridge per 2016 px tile instead: a run of hoops would be overhead in every frame including the one
framing the landmark, and the bridge is the same 'portal the player passes through' that Ottawa validated.
Where it falls, and why it matters: see assets/style/quebec-city-level.md section 3.

BLIND PASS, 2026-09-08. This subject FAILED: the composite read as a frozen ice-covered river, and the built-chute feature was recorded absent. The two causes were in this contract rather than in the drawing - the `ice` ramp on the lane and flat colour-band dividers - and both are corrected above. A previous, primed reading had recorded the same feature PRESENT, which is what a primed reading is worth.

subjects.renderRecipe: UNRENDERED, by decision, and the same decision Ottawa made about its skyline. No source answers this subject. `layer-20-farbank.svg` and `layer-30-river.svg` are a GENERIC winter river town and open water and must stay generic: they are repeating parallax tiles that the low preset drops, and the art bible forbids putting an identifying feature on a droppable layer. A verifier able to name Quebec City from them would be reporting a defect, not a pass. The city's own identifying feature lives in `landmark-chateau-frontenac@1x.svg`, which is judged as `chateau-frontenac`.
subjects.subject: Quebec City seen from across the Saint Lawrence: the Chateau Frontenac on Cap Diamant above the Old Town

mustBeRight.feature: the city stands on a cliff above the river
mustBeRight.why: Cap Diamant is why Quebec City is where it is, and the height is the first thing the view from the water shows.
mustBeRight.detail: A rock bluff with snow on its ledges, rising out of the water, with the town on top rather than beside it.

mustBeRight.feature: the Chateau Frontenac on the skyline, above everything else
mustBeRight.why: From the river it is the one silhouette that names the city.
mustBeRight.detail: Green copper roofs and one dark pyramidal tower, standing clear of the roofline around it. See the chateau-frontenac subject for the measured proportions.

mustBeRight.feature: steep metal roofs on the town below
mustBeRight.why: The vernacular roofline is what places the town in Quebec rather than anywhere else in North America.
mustBeRight.detail: Steep pitched roofs in pale metal with snow on the ridges, dormers, and a parish steeple, packed close. Rhythm, not count.

simplifyAway: individual windows below 6 px
modern towers behind the Old Town
cranes and port machinery
neverAdd: mountains behind the city
a bridge across the river in the same frame as the Old Town
notes: Recorded rather than dropped, so that a later level or a map screen that DOES draw Quebec City from the water
has the contract waiting instead of inventing one. Its lists are dormant while `renders` is empty.

The id avoids ordinary English words on purpose. It was `quebec-city-from-the-river` for one run and the leak scanner in scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs failed the hand-off on the token "from", which the briefing it writes obviously contains. That scanner takes single words from `id` and `expectedBlindAnswer` only, and its own comment says it was narrowed to those because an earlier version fired on "from", "with" and "every" - it assumes those two fields hold only distinctive words. THAT ASSUMPTION IS A CONSTRAINT ON THIS FILE and nothing states it here, so it is stated here: no subject id and no expectedBlindAnswer may contain a common English word of four letters or more. It cost one red run to find.

subjects.subject: A section of a fortified stone city wall in winter
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`, the same builder as chateau-frontenac.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. It is a piece of masonry, and a piece of masonry cannot carry a city. The
place-anchor for this level is chateau-frontenac and nothing else.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY: that the wall is DEFENSIVE. "A garden wall", "a retaining wall", "a dam" or "a
building" is a FAIL. The salient angle, the batter and the height against the snow bank are what
separate a rampart from a wall around a field, and they are the three things drawn hardest.

mustBeRight.feature: two faces meeting at a salient angle, the near face lit and the returning face in shade
mustBeRight.why: A straight wall drawn flat-on is a backdrop. The angle is what says bastion, and it is what the reference photograph is of.
mustBeRight.detail: The corner is a vertical line about a third of the way across the file, with quoin stones marking it. The returning face is drawn in the material’s shade tone, the near face in its base tone, and the coping runs unbroken round the corner so the two faces read as one wall rather than two walls meeting.

mustBeRight.feature: a batter: the wall leans back as it rises, so it is wider at the foot than at the head
mustBeRight.why: Every fortification wall is battered and no garden wall is. It is the cheapest available cue and it costs two degrees of slope.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED by eye on quebec-city/quebec-ramparts-snow.jpg, which is a snow white-out and supports no finer measurement than that: the face leans back by roughly one part in twenty-five. The shipped art draws the head 22 px inboard of the foot over a 320 px rise.

mustBeRight.feature: a plain flat coping along the head, with snow lying on it
mustBeRight.why: It is what the reference shows, and it is the feature most likely to be replaced by an invention.
mustBeRight.detail: One flat capping course projecting slightly over the face, with a shadow line under it, and a band of `snow` on top with a lit crest. NOT crenellated, NOT castellated, NOT pierced.

mustBeRight.feature: coursed masonry drawn as sparse marks, not as a stone pattern
mustBeRight.detail: Five course lines across the near face with staggered vertical joints, all one tone apart from the face and all 6 to 7 px. A drawn stone pattern is forbidden by art-bible section 1, and the first build of this subject had three courses of 12 px and read as a wall of eight enormous bricks.

mustBeRight.feature: a snow bank at the foot, and snow is the ground
mustBeRight.detail: A swept `snow` bank running the width of the file with a lit crest, meeting the file’s bottom edge, which IS the level ground line. The level’s theme.ground is snow-base, so the bank continues into the fill below the line.

simplifyAway: individual stones: five courses and a dozen joints are the whole masonry
mortar joints below 6 px, weathering, lichen and staining
the bare trees, the modern towers and the fog of the reference photograph
the ditch, the glacis and the counterscarp below the snow bank: they are below the ground line and are never drawn
neverAdd: crenellation, battlements, merlons, arrow slits or a machicolation. The wall in the reference has a plain coping and this is the single most likely wrong addition to a fortification in a cartoon
a tower, a turret, a gate, a drawbridge or a portcullis
a cannon, a gun carriage, a pile of shot, a sentry box or any weapon
a flag, a coat of arms, a plaque, a date stone or any lettering in either language
a figure on or in front of the wall

brick. Scoped deliberately: `brick` is required of chateau-frontenac and forbidden here, and the reason is that the two subjects are judged in the same hand-off and a shared ramp would make one read as part of the other
notes: quebec-city/quebec-ramparts-snow.jpg is the only reference and it is a SNOW WHITE-OUT: the air is
full of snow, the contrast is almost gone and the far end of the wall disappears into it. It is a
GEOMETRY AND ARRANGEMENT reference only - the angle, the batter, the plain coping, the snow on top,
the bank at the foot - and every colour in the drawing comes from palette.json. Recorded because the
temptation with a photograph this pale is to sample it, and what it would yield is white.
WHY THIS AND NOT A CANNON OR A GATE. Both were wanted and neither is in any licence-clean photograph
in this repository. The rule that costs this project references is the same rule that stops it
inventing: a thing that exists gets drawn from a reference, and a thing that does not is not drawn.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none, because there is no identification threshold to protect - masonry at 120 px is
masonry. DRAWING OBSERVATION: at 180 px wide the corner, the quoins, the coping, the snow and four of
the five courses are still legible.

subjects.subject: A striped open bandstand kiosk on a winter promenade
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT IS ALLOWED TO BE IDENTIFIED AS A PLACE AND IS NOT REQUIRED TO BE. An unprimed verifier
named Terrasse Dufferin, Quebec City off this exact object when it was drawn into layer-50-terrace.svg,
which is why it is not there any more: that tile REPEATS, and a building that names a city cannot
repeat four times across a level. A POI hero is drawn once, at one place in the world, so here the
same recognisability is an asset rather than a defect.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY is the open pavilion: posts, a balustrade, a dark open interior and a striped
tented roof. "A tent", "a carousel", "a merry-go-round" or "a circus top" is a FAIL - the posts, the
balustrade and the stepped base are what make it built rather than pitched.

mustBeRight.feature: a shallow tented roof of radial green and white stripes
mustBeRight.why: It is the whole silhouette and the whole colour of the object, and it is what a verifier recognised it by.
mustBeRight.detail: Stripes converge on the apex, alternating white and green, drawn as triangles from the apex to the eave. MEASURED on quebec-city/dufferin-terrace-boardwalk.jpg: the roof is about 2.9 times as wide as it is tall from eave to apex, which is a shallow tent and not a cone. The stripes left of the apex take the light tone of each material and those right of it the base or shade, which is the one key light the whole game uses.

mustBeRight.feature: a scalloped valance hanging from the eave, all round
mustBeRight.why: Without it the roof meets the posts in a hard line and the object reads as a bus shelter.
mustBeRight.detail: A continuous run of rounded scallops in one dark tone, about 47 px across each and 24 px deep. They were drawn alternating light and dark for one build and read as holes in the eave.

mustBeRight.feature: an open pavilion: posts, a turned balustrade between them, and a DARK interior behind
mustBeRight.why: A bandstand is open. Filled in, it is a kiosk that sells things; walled, it is a shed.
mustBeRight.detail: Five white posts with a cap and a base block, a balustrade filling the lower half of each bay, and a flat dark field behind all of it so the eye reads through the structure into shadow. The dark is `slate-shade`, not black.

mustBeRight.feature: a stepped base standing clear of the deck, with snow on it
mustBeRight.detail: Two steps, the upper narrower than the lower, in `snow` tones because they are snow-covered. The file’s bottom edge IS the level ground line.

mustBeRight.feature: a plain ball finial at the apex, and nothing else on the roof
mustBeRight.detail: A short post and one ball. No weathervane, no spire, no flag, no lamp.

simplifyAway: the turning of the balusters: two lit bars per bay is the rhythm
the ironwork brackets in the spandrels of the arches
the seats, the electrical fittings and the loudspeakers inside
the ceiling boards: the interior is one flat dark field
the terrace railing, the lamps and the crowd around it: they are on layer-50-terrace.svg, which this hero is drawn in front of
neverAdd: any lettering, sign, date, wordmark or musical notation

a flag or a flagpole. The 1905 photograph shows a Union Flag and a Red Ensign flying beside this kiosk; both are real, both are historic, and OQ-ART-04 - which red is the National Flag - is still open
a band, a conductor, an audience or a figure of any kind
a carousel horse, a ticket window, a counter or a serving hatch: those turn a bandstand into a fairground and it is the nearest wrong reading
snow falling in the file. The level draws snow with Graphics at runtime, procedurally, and a drawn flake would double it
notes: THIS OBJECT HAS A HISTORY IN THIS REPOSITORY AND IT IS THE POINT OF THE SUBJECT. It was drawn into
layer-50-terrace.svg as street furniture; the blind pass of 2026-09-08 named the place off it; the
tile now carries a plain open timber shelter instead and its neverAdd forbids "a recognisable
building of any kind on these repeating tiles, INCLUDING street furniture". That prohibition is
scoped to those tiles, and verifyArtProtocol.contradictionRule is explicit that a prohibition on one
subject may not forbid a requirement of another. The kiosk is required HERE.
quebec-city/dufferin-terrace-boardwalk.jpg is the primary reference - the kiosk in full sun, square
on, with the terrace railing, the lamps and the slide behind it. The 1905 photograph shows the same
kiosk in winter with the crowd and the flags, and is where the winter setting comes from.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw it below 280 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise it.
DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px the stripes, the scallops, the five posts, the
balustrade and the two steps all survive; the 120 px silhouette is a wide shallow cone on an open
colonnade, which is a bandstand and is not a tent.

subjects.subject: The Old Town Clock on Citadel Hill, Halifax
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `singleSource()`, the same builder as peace-tower and chateau-frontenac.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THE KIND OF THING PASSES; THE PLACE NAME IS A BONUS. Amended 2026-09-17: this entry used to accept
only proper nouns, and a blind viewer cannot read a proper noun off a drawing that carries no
lettering - the art rule forbids lettering - so it false-failed a verifier who answered correctly.
The place names stay accepted and naming it is strong positive evidence of real recognition. But a
verifier who answers `a clock tower` has PASSED, and a run that returns only the kind is a finding
about this LEVEL's place anchor, not a defect in this drawing. It is a single non-repeating POI hero drawing one
specific building whose stack - white clapboard box, round colonnade, blue-and-gold dial, arched
belfry, green copper ogee dome, gold ball - is not shared by any other building this game will
ever draw. A verifier who cannot tell it is a CLOCK TOWER is reporting a defect in the drawing;
one who can see that and cannot put a city to it is reporting the limit of what a drawing can say.
IT IS ALSO THE LEVEL'S ONLY ANCHOR THAT CAN. `pier-21` is the level's other hero and is NOT asked
for a place name; `halifax-quayside` is two repeating tiles and is not asked either. So Halifax
as a place rests on this render alone, which is a deliberate structural choice and is stated here
rather than left to be discovered: if this landmark stops identifying, the level stops being
identifiable, and no amount of work on the other two subjects buys it back.

mustBeRight.feature: a deep blue dial with gold hands and gold marks, on a white drum
mustBeRight.why: The single strongest cue, and the pair that stops this landmark and Ottawa's from being the same landmark. The Peace Tower's dial is WHITE on a buff Gothic sandstone shaft; this one is BLUE on white-painted wood under a green copper dome. Drawn in one colour scheme the two levels would have one clock tower between them.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on halifax/town-clock-elevation.jpg (1280x1600, converted from its embedded profile to sRGB before anything was sampled): the dial's centre is at (660, 848), its diameter is about 92 px, and the clock drum it sits on is 185 px wide, so DIAL : DRUM = 0.50. The dial colour is the hue-filtered median of 11500 sunlit dial pixels, #113a7b = hsl(217,76%,27%); `cobalt` was added to palette.json for it at hsl(218,73%,30%), a little lighter so the brass reads at phone size. The shipped art draws the dial at 115 on a 232 drum = 0.496. IT WAS DRAWN AT 0.59 FOR ONE BUILD, on a ratio taken from a colour segmentation that the sky above and the flanking sash windows either side were both contaminating; the number that stuck was read off a labelled grid crop of the same file, where what is being measured can be seen.

mustBeRight.feature: a green copper ogee dome under a small balustraded cupola and a gold ball
mustBeRight.why: The top of the silhouette, and the second thing a person uses to recognise it. A hemispherical dome or a pointed spire in its place changes the building.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED by copper-hue segmentation on halifax/town-clock-elevation.jpg, which is the one measurement on this subject a segmentation could make cleanly because nothing else in the frame is that hue: the dome occupies rows 600..700 and columns 567..751, so 185 wide by 100 tall - HEIGHT : WIDTH = 0.54, and WIDTH = 0.298 of the base building.
