level - the same finding the Quebec City terrace kiosk produced, arrived at from the other direction,
and it is why that clause now names this subject as the place the object belongs.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none is set; a cable fan at 120 px is still a cable fan. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an
identification: at 180 px wide the mast, all eight cables, the rail posts, the pier and the water are
still legible; the 120 px silhouette is a leaning mast over a horizontal deck, which is the subject.

subjects.subject: A maple tree in full autumn colour, with fallen leaves at its foot
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THE WORD THAT MATTERS IS MAPLE, and it is the only thing this subject is really asking. "A tree" alone
is a partial answer: the five fallen leaves on the paving are drawn at 48 to 60 px precisely so the
species is legible, because the fact this POI carries is about the maple leaf and a generic tree would
teach it by assertion.
IT IS NOT AN EMBLEM AND MUST NOT READ AS ONE. If an identifier says "the Canadian flag", "a maple leaf
logo" or "a national symbol on a field", that is a FAIL and it means the leaves have been drawn as a
device rather than as litter on the ground. They are scattered, at five different angles, none of them
centred, none of them on a panel, and there is no red-white-red field anywhere in the file.
FOUR ORDINARY ENGLISH WORDS ARE DELIBERATELY ABSENT FROM THE ANSWERS ON THIS AND THREE OTHER SUBJECTS
ADDED ON 2026-09-13: "tree", "with", "over" and "small". The hand-off's own READ-ME-FIRST.txt contains
all four as ordinary English, and scripts/verify-art.mjs's leak check - which searches every handed-over
text for any token from any accepted answer - reported them the moment these subjects were added. None of
them is a leak: the text predates the answers. The fix the gate itself names in that case is to reword the
answer, so "a maple tree" is "a maple", "a rail fence with a gate" is "a gate hung in a rail fence", and
so on. The identification each answer demands is unchanged; only the connective words are.

mustBeRight.feature: a broad rounded crown, wider than it is tall, on a short trunk
mustBeRight.why: It is the proportion of a street maple in a city park and it is what stops the subject reading as a conifer or a poplar.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED against the autumn trees in winnipeg/cmhr-from-the-forks-tower.jpg: crown width is about 1.3 times crown height and the clear trunk is about a quarter of the total. The shipped art draws a 520 px crown 400 px tall on a 640 px file with 190 px of clear trunk. The crown is built from overlapping rounded lobes rather than one ellipse, because one ellipse is what the parallax tile already draws three of.

mustBeRight.feature: autumn colour in three tones of ONE red ramp, lit upper left
mustBeRight.why: Two ramps in a canopy reads as two trees behind each other. The variation that makes foliage look like foliage is the light, not the hue.
mustBeRight.detail: The `oxide` ramp and nothing else: the lit lobes upper left, the base through the middle, the shade lobes lower right. NOT `flag-red`, which is the flag's red and is not what a leaf is, and NOT the ochre the parallax tile's trees use - the hero has to be distinguishable from them at a glance.

mustBeRight.feature: fallen maple leaves on the ground, drawn as maple leaves
mustBeRight.why: This is the feature the subject exists for. A generic oval leaf teaches nothing and a five-lobed maple leaf teaches the fact the POI carries.
mustBeRight.detail: Five leaves, 48 to 60 px across, each with the five lobes and the deep sinuses of a maple, each at a different angle, scattered around the tree pit and not arranged. Two lit, two base, one shade, from the same `oxide` ramp as the crown.

mustBeRight.feature: a kerbed tree pit of bare soil
mustBeRight.why: It is what a street tree stands in, it grounds the trunk on paving, and it is what says CITY rather than forest.
mustBeRight.detail: A shallow elliptical kerb in `limestone` with a lit top edge, filled with `wood-shade` soil. The file's bottom edge IS the level ground line and the paving around it is the plaza tile's.

mustBeRight.feature: three heavy branches visible where the crown meets the trunk
mustBeRight.detail: Two spreading and one rising, thick enough to survive 25 per cent - none under 18 px - and drawn BEHIND the crown lobes so only their bases show.

simplifyAway: individual leaves in the crown: the lobes are the foliage, and a drawn leaf pattern is the surface pattern art-bible section 1 forbids
bark texture, knots and lenticels
twigs, seed keys and anything else under 12 px
a second and third tree: the parallax tile behind already carries three
grass: this tree stands in paving, which is what the level's promenade is
neverAdd: a flag, a flagpole, a banner, a shield or any panel with a leaf on it
a single large centred maple leaf anywhere in the file
lettering, a dedication plaque or a tree label of any kind
snow or bare branches: this level is early autumn and it is the only autumn level in the game
a bench, a lamp or a bin: the plaza tile already draws all three and a hero that repeats them steals the tile's rhythm
a figure, for the reason cable-stayed-bridge gives
notes: NO PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE SPECIFIC TREE IS BEING COPIED, and that is stated rather than left to be found.
The two Winnipeg references establish the SEASON and the SETTING - a promenade of street trees in full
autumn colour beside the river - and the tree is drawn as a type to the scale those photographs give.
A tree is a type in the way a bench is a type, and this project already draws three of them into
winnipeg/layer-40-plaza.svg without a reference for any individual one.
WHY A TREE IS A POINT OF INTEREST. It carries a sourced fact - Discover Canada page 79, the maple leaf
is Canada's best-known symbol - and the brief this work is done under is explicit that a point of
interest is something a player can stop at and learn one sourced fact from, not necessarily a landmark.
It is also the only object in the game that can carry that fact without drawing the flag, which
OQ-ART-04 has kept open since slice 1.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw it below 280 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise the leaves.
DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px the lobed crown, the three tones, the trunk, the
pit and four of the five fallen leaves survive; at 120 px as a silhouette it is a broad crown on a
short trunk, which is a tree and is not a lamp, a kiosk or a person.

subjects.subject: A wooden prairie grain elevator beside a railway track
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT MAY NOT DEMAND A PLACE NAME, and the reason is the same one that governs `pier-21`.
Every wooden prairie elevator carries its company's name and its town's name painted across the crib -
PIONEER and CHAMBERLAIN on the reference this one is drawn from, SASKATCHEWAN and SINTALUTA on the
second - and `make verify-art` refuses any render source containing a <text> element, because a name
drawn into the picture defeats every byte-level leak check in the hand-off. So the elevator ships
blank, and what is left is the STANDARD PLAN that stood in a thousand prairie towns: a type.
`Saskatchewan`, `the Prairies` and any town name are therefore NOT in the accepted list and the gate
MUST NOT reward them. A verifier who names a province from this render has inferred it; a verifier who
says `a grain elevator` has seen what is drawn.
THE CONSEQUENCE IS STRUCTURAL AND IS STATED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE DISCOVERED. Level 7 is a REGION,
not a town, and nothing in its art is asked to name a place - not this hero and not
`prairie-rail-line`. That is a deliberate choice and not an omission: the level's subject is Modern
Canada and its setting is the plains, and the only honest anchor a plains level has is the type.

mustBeRight.feature: a tall gable-roofed CRIB, well over twice as tall as it is wide
mustBeRight.why: It is the whole silhouette. Below about 1 : 2 the building stops being an elevator and becomes a barn.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED TWICE AND THE TWO AGREE. On prairie-rail/grain-elevator-chamberlain.jpg the crib is 380 px wide and 870 px from the ground to the gable apex; on prairie-rail/grain-elevator-sintaluta-elevation.jpg the same figures are 270 and 615. HEIGHT : WIDTH = 2.29 and 2.28. The shipped art is 280 x 638 = 2.28. Gable rise 0.30 of the crib width, which is the MEAN of the two references' 0.25 and 0.35 and is recorded as a mean rather than left looking like a measurement.

mustBeRight.feature: a CUPOLA straddling the ridge, narrower than the crib and rising well above it
mustBeRight.why: It is the head house that carries the leg, it is the second thing a person recognises, and a gabled box with no cupola is a shed.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on the Sintaluta elevation, which is the near-orthographic one: the cupola is 0.30 of the crib width across and rises 0.44 of the crib width above the gable apex. It has its own small gable roof and a vent above it.

mustBeRight.feature: a LOW driveway annex along one side, with a shed roof falling away from the crib and an opening a truck drives into
mustBeRight.why: The tall-box-and-long-low-shed pair is the elevator's whole asymmetry. A crib standing alone reads as a tower.
mustBeRight.detail: 1.45 crib widths long, 1.00 crib widths tall where it meets the crib and 0.52 at the far end. Chamberlain's apparent length is 1.68 crib widths and is NOT used: that photograph is taken close and low and the annex recedes hard away from the camera, so its apparent length is a projection.

mustBeRight.feature: painted timber in a strong red oxide, with contrasting ochre trim on the gable edge and the eaves
mustBeRight.why: It is what says painted wooden building rather than concrete terminal, and the trim band is the elevator's one piece of colour.
mustBeRight.detail: `oxide` is its own palette ramp, base #91301c = hsl(11,68%,34%), authored as the HSL midpoint of the two large measured faces on the Chamberlain reference: the sunlit annex at hsl(8,73%,36%) and the shaded crib gable at hsl(13,63%,32%). NOT `brick`, whose base is hsl(17,52%,44%) - eight degrees more orange, sixteen points less saturated and ten points lighter, which turns a painted elevator into a masonry wall. Trim is `brass`.

mustBeRight.feature: a loading spout reaching out from the cupola toward the track side
mustBeRight.detail: A slanted steel tube from the head house down to a spout head, over a low track-side annex. It is what the building is FOR, and without it the crib is a grain bin with a hat.

mustBeRight.feature: it stands in gravel beside a rail, not on grass and not on a street
mustBeRight.detail: A ballast apron with a siding rail across the foot of the file, and weeds at its back edge. prairie-rail/grain-elevator-govan-and-track.jpg shows exactly this relationship from beside the line.

simplifyAway: the board-and-batten boarding: it is a surface pattern, and art-bible section 1 forbids drawing one
the man-lift, the ladders, the catwalks and the guy wires
the external cyclone and dust pipe on the Chamberlain reference: it is unusual to that building and reads as a chimney
the individual sash bars of the crib windows: one dark pane with an ochre head
the steel bins, the driveway scale and the seed-cleaning plant that stand beside most surviving elevators

the company name and the town name painted across the crib, and the star or shield device beside them: they are the two most identifying things on the real building and this project draws no lettering
neverAdd: any lettering, wordmark, company name, town name or number, in either language
an invented company name or an invented device in place of the real one: art-bible's `drop, never substitute`, and an approximated livery mark is worse than none
a concrete terminal, a slip-form silo or a row of steel bins as the main mass: those are the modern replacement and are a different building
a barn: no hip roof, no cupola with louvres on a wide low mass, no hayloft door
mountains or foothills on the horizon behind it: that is level 8's picture, not this one
any depiction of a person, a pattern or an object belonging to any nation named in this level's territory statement
notes: prairie-rail/grain-elevator-chamberlain.jpg is CC0 and is the building this is drawn from: the
surviving Pioneer elevator at Chamberlain, Saskatchewan. It is the reference for the livery, the trim,
the driveway and the arrangement, and for the crib's height : width. It is taken close and from below,
so it is NOT the reference for the annex's length.
prairie-rail/grain-elevator-sintaluta-elevation.jpg is the near-orthographic one and is the reference
for the cupola's proportions and for the second, agreeing, height : width measurement.
prairie-rail/grain-elevator-govan-and-track.jpg shows a surviving elevator beside the main line with
the prairie running to the horizon behind it, and is the reference for the SETTING and for the fact
that the gable end and the annex flank really are both visible from beside the track.
prairie-rail/grain-elevators-mossleigh-elevation.jpg and prairie-rail/prairie-elevator-from-the-train.jpg
are the cross-checks: three elevators in a row and one seen from a moving train, both near-orthographic.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw this landmark below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise
it. The verifier's floor from Ottawa, adopted rather than re-derived. As a DRAWING OBSERVATION and
explicitly not an identification: at 250 px the crib, the cupola, the annex and the spout are all still
separable and the trim still reads as trim.
The two-size test in art-bible section 5 was run at the shipping size of 900 x 1000 and passed at both
probes. The measured saving from pinning it to 1x is 13.73 MiB -> 3.43 MiB of decoded texture.

subjects.subject: A single-track railway line running across open prairie
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the fields ABOVE the railbed and the railbed drawn over them where they overlap, which is the order the level uses. In world coordinates the railbed tile's top edge is 210 px ABOVE the fields tile's top edge (world y 800 against 1010), so the offset is NEGATIVE: `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'fields', nearMatch: 'railbed', nearTop: -210 })`. Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 1920) rather than laying them side by side. Neither file answers the subject alone: a track with nothing behind it is a track anywhere, and a field with no track is a field.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. Both tiles repeat - 1800 and 1920 - so neither may carry anything that identifies a
place, and in particular neither carries a grain elevator: that is the level's only non-repeating
anchor and it lives on `grain-elevator`. A verifier who names a province from these two tiles would be
reporting a defect.
`railroad` and `railroad track` are accepted alongside `railway`, and this is the amendment
`toronto-trail` needed after a blind pass failed on `bicycle` when only `bike` and `cycle` were listed.
The rule stated once: an expectedBlindAnswer list is a VOCABULARY for one picture, and a list that
omits a plain word for the thing drawn measures the verifier's diction rather than the art. `a road`,
`a path`, `a tram line` and `a level crossing` alone do not pass: the last one names the furniture and
not the line.
THE PRAIRIE IS NOT ASKED FOR. `across the prairie` is in the list because a verifier who says it is not
wrong, and it is NOT required: flat farmland under a big sky is flat farmland under a big sky, and the
art may not be scored on an inference.

mustBeRight.feature: two rails on timber ties over a ballast shoulder, running the full width
mustBeRight.why: It is the subject. One rail is a fence, and rails without ties are a pipeline.
mustBeRight.detail: Forty ties on a 48 px period - 1920 / 48 = 40 exactly, so the rhythm survives the tile seam - two rails, and a ballast shoulder drawn as scattered chips rather than a texture fill. The near rail head is the level's ground line.

mustBeRight.feature: a red-edged white CROSSBUCK and a two-lens flashing-light mast at a gravel crossing
mustBeRight.why: It is the one object in this level that says RAILWAY without a word on it, which is exactly what a project that draws no lettering needs, and it is what stops the track reading as a tramway or a mine road.
mustBeRight.detail: Two white boards crossed at about 26 degrees with a red border, on a white mast, under a black backing board carrying two red lenses. NO LETTERING: a real Canadian crossbuck carries words and this one carries none, which is a deliberate omission and not an oversight. A gravel section road crosses behind it and the crossing deck runs over the ties.

mustBeRight.feature: timber telegraph poles with crossarms and drooping wires, on a strict repeating period
mustBeRight.why: The level's locomotion is `train` and the camera does all the work: the pole rhythm is what makes movement legible, and it is the oldest visual shorthand there is for a railway on a plain.
mustBeRight.detail: Four poles on a 480 px period - 1920 / 480 = 4 exactly - each with a crossarm, four glass insulators and three drooping catenary wires into the next bay.

mustBeRight.feature: harvested field in SWATHS, laid at a slight angle to the track
mustBeRight.why: Parallel bands alone read as a striped rug. A cut crop lying in rows at an angle is what a prairie field looks like from a train, and it is what makes this farmland rather than grassland.
mustBeRight.detail: Fourteen long cut rows across the fields tile, each with its own shadow line, over bands of standing swath, cut stubble and a grass headland. Straw is the `felt` ramp, measured at hsl(38,63%,33%) on prairie-rail/prairie-harvest-and-shelterbelt.jpg.

mustBeRight.feature: a poplar shelterbelt in broken clumps with real gaps, not a continuous hedge
mustBeRight.detail: Four clumps to the tile with gaps between them. A continuous row reads as a hedge and closes the horizon, which is the one thing a prairie level cannot afford.

simplifyAway: the rail's web and foot profile: two flat bars with a lit top arris
tie plates, spikes, joint bars and ballast between the ties
the insulators' individual caps below 8 px
the fence's staples and the wire's sag between posts
the crossing signal's bell, its gate arm and its cabinet
neverAdd: a grain elevator ON EITHER OF THESE TWO REPEATING TILES: it is required on the `grain-elevator` subject and forbidden here, and the reason is the tiling, not the building
any lettering, number plate, whistle post, mile board or signage, in either language

a locomotive or rolling stock ON EITHER OF THESE TWO REPEATING TILES: a train drawn on a tile repeats with it, every 1920 px. The rideable level object this entry once waited for now exists - the `park-car` subject, a ride the engine places at the player (ADR-0031), with the rig's seated `train/` poses - and it is still never scenery in this subject
overhead electrification, a catenary mast or a third rail: this is a diesel-worked prairie branch
mountains or foothills on the horizon: that is level 8's picture

a second track, a turnout or a signal gantry ON EITHER TILE: each tile carries one track. The level as a whole now shows two - the ride's main line in the foreground and these tiles' rails behind it, which read as the siding the container car and the elevator stand on - and that second line belongs to the ride, not to this subject
any depiction of a person, a pattern or an object belonging to any nation named in this level's territory statement
notes: prairie-rail/grain-elevator-govan-and-track.jpg is the primary reference: single track, ballast
shoulder, a siding, a wire fence and the prairie running flat to the horizon, all in one frame.
prairie-rail/prairie-harvest-and-shelterbelt.jpg is the reference for the swaths, the stubble bands
and the shelterbelt line; prairie-rail/prairie-elevator-from-the-train.jpg is the reference for what
the level's own viewpoint actually looks like, because it was taken from one.
prairie-rail/prairie-freight-train-at-dawn.jpg shows a freight beside an elevator and is the reference
for the track's relationship to the buildings. It is NOT a colour reference: it is a winter dawn.
THE SKY AND THE FAR HORIZON ARE NOT PART OF THIS SUBJECT. layer-10-sky.svg and layer-20-horizon.svg are
drawn, credited and shipped and are asked no question: one is a flat field with clouds and the other is
a distant shelterbelt and two farmsteads, and neither has a feature that could identify anything.
THE TRAIN IS NOT PART OF THIS SUBJECT EITHER. Since 2026-09-14 the level draws the player riding the
rear car of VIA Rail's Canadian on a nearer line in the foreground (ADR-0031, assets/style/prairie-rail-level.md
section 13). That car is `park-car` and is judged on its own; these two tiles are still judged as a
railway across the prairie with nothing on it, which is what they draw.

subjects.subject: A row of hopper-bottom steel farm grain bins
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`, the same builder as grain-elevator.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE: these are farm bins, not a named facility, and the level's place-anchor is
grain-elevator. No answer here names a province.
THE FAILURE THIS SUBJECT WAS REDRAWN FOUR TIMES TO AVOID IS "houses", "a village", "barns" or "a
farmyard". Three builds of this render read as a row of gabled buildings, because a triangle on a
rectangle is a house whatever the shading does. What fixed it is in the first two mustBeRight entries
and it is structural rather than decorative: the bins stand OFF the ground on legs, with a funnel
under each one and daylight under that. A bin drawn sitting on the ground is a building.

mustBeRight.feature: each bin stands clear of the ground on legs, over a funnel-shaped hopper, with a dark void under it
mustBeRight.why: It is the whole identification. Nothing else in this game is a cylinder held in the air on legs, and no house is.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED off a 280 x 130 crop of prairie-rail/prairie-freight-train-at-dawn.jpg enlarged four times, which is the only view of these bins in the repository: the hopper and the leg gap together are about a quarter of the total height. Three legs per bin, thin, dark, standing on the pad, with the funnel narrowing to a small throat between them.

mustBeRight.feature: a STEEP conical roof, taller than a house roof and pointed, with a small peak vent
mustBeRight.detail: The cone is roughly 0.5 of the bin's diameter in height - much steeper than the shallow cone a first build drew - and it overhangs the body by a small eave. One small vent cap at the apex and nothing else on it: no cupola, no dormer, no chimney.

mustBeRight.feature: tall narrow corrugated cylinders, ringed by horizontal seams
mustBeRight.why: A bin is taller than it is wide, which is the opposite of the proportion two builds of this drawing used. The rings are what corrugated steel looks like at this scale, and they are the only surface marking allowed.
mustBeRight.detail: Body height about 1.4 times the diameter. Four to six horizontal ring seams, full width, evenly spaced - rhythm, not count - and three flat vertical tone bands for the cylinder, lit on the left. NO vertical corrugation lines: that is the surface pattern art-bible section 1 forbids.

mustBeRight.feature: four bins of different heights in a row, one carrying a ladder
mustBeRight.why: One bin alone reads as a silo; a row of them reads as a farm's grain storage, which is what the POI teaches.
mustBeRight.detail: Different heights and diameters, overlapping slightly, the tallest nearest the centre. One vertical ladder of two stiles and evenly spaced rungs on the tallest.

mustBeRight.feature: a gravel pad under them
mustBeRight.detail: A flat band of `path` with a lit top edge and a few darker scatter marks. The file's bottom edge IS the level ground line.

simplifyAway: the corrugation itself: the ring seams are the whole surface
augers, fill pipes, aeration fans and the electrical gear at the base
the manhole, the roof ladder and the safety cage
the fifth bin and everything behind the row
neverAdd: a company name, a co-operative mark, a wordmark, a number or any lettering in either language

a wooden elevator in the same frame. Scoped deliberately: the tall timber elevator with a cupola is REQUIRED on grain-elevator and forbidden here, because the two subjects are judged in the same hand-off and this one must not be able to answer for that one
a gabled roof, a door with a frame, a window or a porch: every one of those turns a bin into a building, and three builds of this render did exactly that
a figure, a truck or a tractor
snow: this level is late summer
notes: THIS SUBJECT TOOK FOUR BUILDS AND THE FIRST THREE ARE THE FINDING. Build one drew trapezoid roofs on
rectangles and read as a row of houses. Build two made the cones steeper and the read did not change.
Build three added a reflected-light rim at the far edge of each cylinder - the standard trick for
making a cylinder read - and it STILL read as houses, because the shading was never the problem: the
silhouette was. Build four put the bins on legs over hoppers, which is what the reference shows and
what no building has, and the read changed at once. Recorded because the same mistake is available on
every cylindrical subject this game will ever draw.
prairie-rail/prairie-freight-train-at-dawn.jpg is a DAWN exposure - the sky is orange and magenta and
everything below it is in silhouette - so it is a GEOMETRY reference only and every colour here comes
from palette.json.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px wide the legs, the
hoppers, the cones, the vents and the ring seams all survive; the 120 px silhouette is a row of
pointed cylinders standing on legs.

subjects.subject: A combine harvester in standing grain
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswer: a combine in a wheat field
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE: no make, no model and no maker's badge, and the level's place-anchor is
grain-elevator.
"A tractor" is a FAIL and it is the near miss this subject is drawn against. A tractor has no header,
no reel and no grain tank; the wide cutting front with the slatted reel turning above a pale cutter
bar is what makes this machine a combine, and it is why the header is drawn at full size on the right
of the frame with clear air around it rather than tucked behind the drive wheel, which is where a
first build put it.

mustBeRight.feature: a wide header at the front, lower than the body, carrying a slatted reel above a pale cutter bar
mustBeRight.why: It is the identification. Everything else on the machine is shared with a truck or a tractor.
mustBeRight.detail: The header is about a quarter of the machine's length and sits at knee height to the body. The reel is drawn from the side as a hub with six radial bats standing clear of it, in a tan tone that is not the body red, and the cutter bar under it is a pale steel bar running the full width of the header and a little past it.

mustBeRight.feature: one large drive wheel forward and one small wheel aft
mustBeRight.why: The wheel pair is upside down compared with every road vehicle, and that alone says farm machine.
mustBeRight.detail: The front wheel is about 1.5 times the diameter of the rear one and sits under the cab. Both are dark with a lighter hub. No tread pattern: art-bible section 1 forbids a surface pattern and a drawn tread at this size is noise.

mustBeRight.feature: a high glazed cab set forward, over the drive wheel
mustBeRight.detail: A dark frame with one large pale glazed panel and one mullion, under a pale roof cap. NO figure inside: this level's people are on the parallax tiles and a driver drawn at hero scale would be a second canon.

mustBeRight.feature: an open grain tank on top and an unloading auger folded up and out over one side
mustBeRight.why: The auger is the second-strongest cue after the header and it is what a person remembers about the silhouette.
mustBeRight.detail: A raised open-topped tank along the roof line, and a straight tube rising from it out over the left of the frame at about 20 degrees, with a square spout head at its end.

mustBeRight.feature: it stands in grain: cut stubble in front, standing crop behind
mustBeRight.detail: Bands of the `felt` and `wood` ramps at the bottom of the file with a few swath lines, pale where the crop is standing and darker where it is cut. The file's bottom edge IS the level ground line.

simplifyAway: the badge, the model number, the maker's decals and the warning labels
the ladder, the handrails, the mirrors and the lights
the tread blocks on both tyres
the dust cloud behind it: it is the one thing the reference photograph is mostly made of, and a drawn dust cloud at this scale is a grey smear
the grain cart and the trucks beside it in the reference: one machine is the subject
neverAdd: a badge, a wordmark, a model number, a maker's stripe or any lettering in either language
a figure in the cab or on the ladder
a plough, a seed drill, a baler or a front loader: each one moves this subject to a different machine

a green body. Scoped deliberately rather than stylistically: the reference shows a red machine, and green is the other maker's colour, so drawing it green would assert a brand this render has no reference for
smoke or exhaust
notes: prairie-rail/prairie-harvest-and-shelterbelt.jpg is the only reference: two red machines and a grain
cart working a wheat field under a dust cloud, at a distance, with a shelterbelt on the horizon. It
settles the PROPORTIONS, the wheel arrangement, the colour and the setting, and nothing finer - the
machines in it are about 160 px wide. The drawing does not pretend past that.
THE RED IS THE REFERENCE'S, NOT A BRAND'S. It is drawn from the `oxide` ramp, which this game also
uses for Peggy's Cove's fish stores and Ottawa's warming hut; no badge, stripe or decal is drawn, so
nothing here names a manufacturer.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw it below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise the
header. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px the reel bats, the cutter bar, the cab,
the auger and both wheels survive; the 120 px silhouette is a tall body over two unequal wheels with a
low arm reaching forward, which is a combine and is not a truck.

subjects.subject: A double-stack container car standing on a siding
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswer: a train car carrying shipping containers
a rail car carrying two containers
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE AND MORE STRICTLY THAN MOST. Real containers and real cars are covered in reporting
marks, numbers and owners' liveries, and every one of those would name a company. This one carries
none, and its two box colours are palette ramps chosen against the level's sky rather than any
operator's.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY: that the boxes are on a RAILWAY car. "Shipping containers" alone is a partial
answer and "a truck" is a fail - the trucks, the wheels, the rail and the ties under it are drawn at
full contrast for exactly that reason.

mustBeRight.feature: two containers, one seated IN a dropped well and one stacked on top of it
mustBeRight.why: The double stack is the whole subject: a single box on a flat car is a flat car, and the dropped well is what makes a double stack possible.
mustBeRight.detail: The car's deck is visibly lower between its two ends than at them, the lower box sits down inside it with the car's ends standing proud either side, and the upper box sits squarely on the lower one. The upper box is a little shorter than the lower, which is what the reference shows.

mustBeRight.feature: each box is a plain ribbed rectangle with corner castings and a darker end
mustBeRight.detail: Vertical ribs on a regular period across the side - rhythm, not count - a darker band top and bottom, a darker panel at each end for the doors, and small dark blocks at the four corners. No door hardware below 12 px.

mustBeRight.feature: two four-wheel trucks under the car, on rail
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes the object a railway vehicle and not a lorry trailer or a stack in a yard.
mustBeRight.detail: A dark bogie frame at each end carrying two visible wheels with lighter hubs, sitting on a rail head with ties and ballast below it. The rail head IS the file's ground line, because that is where this level's ground polyline sits.

mustBeRight.feature: the car is at rest
mustBeRight.detail: No motion lines, no dust, no locomotive, no coupling to anything off-frame. The level's locomotion is `train` and since 2026-09-14 the player is drawn riding one - a stainless passenger car on the main line in the foreground (`park-car`, ADR-0031) - while this freight car stands on the siding beyond it; a hero that looked like a moving train would be read as part of the player's own.

simplifyAway: reporting marks, numbers, owners' liveries and every other marking, which is most of what is on a real container
the corrugation of the box skin: a few ribs are the whole surface
brake gear, air hoses, couplers and the slack adjusters
the rest of the train: the reference shows a hundred cars and this is one
neverAdd: any wordmark, reporting mark, number, flag or logo in either language
a locomotive, a caboose or a second car
a grain hopper in the same frame: the level already teaches grain twice and the point of this subject is TRADE

a level crossing, a crossbuck or a signal. Scoped deliberately: a grade crossing with a crossbuck and a flashing-light mast is drawn on prairie-rail/layer-40-railbed.svg, which repeats every 1920 px, and a second one on a hero would double it
a figure on or beside the car
notes: prairie-rail/prairie-freight-train-at-dawn.jpg shows the freight standing beside the elevator at dawn,
in near silhouette against an orange sky. It settles the ARRANGEMENT - a long string of well cars with
boxes stacked two high - and nothing about colour, so the colours are palette ramps.
WHY A CONTAINER AND NOT A GRAIN HOPPER. A hopper would have been the obvious prairie choice and it is
the wrong one twice over: this level already teaches grain at two other points, and Canada's
government grain hoppers carry a livery and a maple leaf device that this project does not draw
(OQ-ART-04). A container teaches the fact this POI carries - Canada is a trading nation - without
asserting anything about whose box it is.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px wide the two boxes, the
dropped well, both bogies, four wheels and the rail all survive; the 120 px silhouette is two stacked
rectangles on a low frame over four wheels.

subjects.subject: The rear car of a stainless-steel passenger train, with a rounded observation end and a glass dome on its roof
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x with `singleSource()`. It is the front layer of the Prairies ride (ADR-0031): the engine draws the player BEHIND this file, seated in the dome, so the file's dome is EMPTY and this render shows the car without its passenger. That is deliberate. The seated rider is the rig's (`train/*` in rig-contract.json) and a ride subject built with a pose would fall under the hand-off's mounted-subject rules, which require `{mode}` equipment frames that a ride by definition does not have; `verify-art` reports `train` as a posed mode with no subject, and that report is the true statement.
expectedBlindAnswer: the rear car of a passenger train
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE, AND THE PLACE IS NOT ASKED FOR. The car is drawn from VIA Rail's Canadian and carries
none of what names it on the real train: no wordmark, no logo, no car name and no number. A verifier who
says VIA Rail or the Canadian has inferred it from a blue band, a dome and a rounded end, and is not wrong,
and it is NOT required: the subject is a passenger car that a person rides, which is the whole of what the
level needs the picture to say.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY: PASSENGER. `a freight car`, `a tanker`, `a bus` and `a subway car` are fails - the
windows, the dome and the observation end are drawn at full contrast for exactly that reason.

mustBeRight.feature: a rounded observation end, with the blue band sweeping round it and a red marker light on top
mustBeRight.why: It is the Park car's silhouette and the one shape no other car in the train has. A flat end with a diaphragm is any coach.
mustBeRight.detail: The roof rolls down over the end on a large radius, the band follows it round, the lower body's corner is rounded, a big end window sits in the upper body and a red marker light stands on the roof at the end. park-car-observation-end-jasper.jpg shows all five from one corner.

mustBeRight.feature: a raised glass dome on the roof, clear enough to see through
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes this a passenger observation car rather than a coach, and it is where the player is seen riding: a head and shoulders through the glass, against the sky.
mustBeRight.detail: A band of glass on a stainless plinth, sloped at both ends under a stainless cap, just ahead of the observation end as both Jasper references show. The glass is a 16 percent sky tint, not a colour, because the rider is drawn behind this file; the mullions are placed clear of the seat so none crosses the rider's face.

mustBeRight.feature: a pale stainless body with horizontal flutes below a row of windows
mustBeRight.why: Fluted stainless steel is what the Budd cars are, and it is what separates this train from a painted one.
mustBeRight.detail: Five flute lines on the lower body, a smooth window band above a belt line, dark glass windows with a single sky glint each, and a door near the forward end.

mustBeRight.feature: one blue letterboard band the length of the car, under the roof
mustBeRight.why: It is the livery's one colour, and a livery colour is not a mark: the same permission the elevator's ochre trim has.
mustBeRight.detail: VIA blue drawn from `cobalt`, with a darker lower edge and a pale top edge; nothing written in it.

mustBeRight.feature: two four-wheel trucks under the car, over a rail
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes it a railway vehicle, and the wheels meeting the ride's track is what makes the rider read as carried rather than floating.
mustBeRight.detail: A dark frame and two wheels with lighter hubs at each truck, the rear one under the observation end, standing on the row the ride's track strip puts its rail head on.

simplifyAway: the car's length: a Park car is about six times as long as it is tall, and this one is compressed so the observation end, the dome and the car ahead share one screen
the full depth of the fluting: five lines stand for it
the dome's curved upper panes, merged into one band of glass under the cap
the vestibule steps, the underframe equipment, the brake rigging and the diaphragm's folds below its outline
the second marker light and the end's lower lights
neverAdd: any wordmark, logo, car name, number or lettering in either language, including the wordmark and the logo every reference carries
a flag decal
a locomotive or a second dome: neither is at the rear of this train
a figure drawn into the file: the passenger is the player, posed by the rig and drawn behind the car at run time
any depiction of a person, a pattern or an object belonging to any nation named in this level's territory statement
notes: prairie-rail/park-car-side-and-dome-jasper.jpg and prairie-rail/park-car-observation-end-jasper.jpg are
CC BY 2.0, by David Wilson, Jasper, Alberta, 2013, and are the references for the observation end, the
band, the marker light and where the dome sits. prairie-rail/canadian-side-elevation-1981.jpg is public
domain, a Roger Puta photograph, and is the near-orthographic view the side is proportioned from. Its
letterboard band is a darker blue-grey under a 1981 winter sky and is NOT a colour reference.
WHY THE REAR CAR, AND WHY THE DOME. The Park car is the car at the tail of the Canadian, so the rider
sits in the last car and the observation end is on screen whenever the train is at rest or cruising.
The dome is where a passenger is visible from outside at 390 px; a head at a side window is a dark
square with a dot in it.
WHERE IT RUNS. On a nearer line than the level's walking line, so the landmarks and the guide stand
beyond it: rendered at 390 px on the walking line, the car hid the container car and the guide at the
moment the train stopped for them. assets/style/prairie-rail-level.md section 13 has the numbers.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none; the car is drawn at 1x at the player every frame. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an
identification: at 390 px the dome, the observation end, the band, the windows and both trucks all
survive, and the rider's head and shoulders read through the glass.

subjects.subject: A working cattle ranch in the Alberta foothills: a red board-sided gable barn with a louvred ridge cupola, a peeled-log corral and a work horse. Drawn from the Bar U Ranch National Historic Site at Longview, Alberta.
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `singleSource()`, the same builder as peace-tower, chateau-frontenac, town-clock, cn-tower, human-rights-museum and grain-elevator.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT MAY NOT DEMAND A PLACE NAME, and the reason is the one that governs `pier-21` and
`grain-elevator`. A ranch barn is a standard timber building type that stood across western North
America; nothing drawn says which country it is in, let alone which province. `Alberta`, `the
foothills` and any town name are NOT in the accepted list and the gate MUST NOT reward them. A
verifier who names a province here has inferred it from project context, which is the mistake the
Ottawa canal subject made and had to be amended for.
WHAT IT MAY DEMAND IS THE WORD RANCH, and that IS a measurement rather than a preference. The render
draws a barn AND a corral AND a horse inside the corral, and those three together are what separates
a ranch from a farm. So `a red barn`, `a barn` and `a farm` alone do NOT pass: an answer naming only
the building is a true report that the corral and the horse did not carry, which is information about
the drawing and is what this gate is for. Every accepted phrase names the enclosure or the word ranch.
THE CONSEQUENCE IS STRUCTURAL. Level 8 is a REGION and nothing in its art is asked to name a place -
not this hero and not `alberta-foothills-rangeland`. The Rocky Mountain front IS in the level, on
layer 20, and is not a graded subject: it repeats and the low preset drops it.

mustBeRight.feature: red-oxide painted timber walls
mustBeRight.why: Barn red on a gable barn is the strongest single colour cue this subject has.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED 2026-09-09, six medians across three references: work-horse-barn-elevation.jpg at (500,715) hsl(4,56%,21%) and (900,760) hsl(4,50%,21%); work-horse-barn-gable-end.jpg at (1080,430) hsl(7,54%,18%) and (1250,430) hsl(3,52%,22%); percheron-at-the-barn-wall.jpg at (60,250) hsl(8,51%,26%) and (360,230) hsl(5,37%,23%). Median hsl(5,51%,21%). All three photographs are late evening or overcast, so the sample sits about 13 points of lightness below the material. Drawn in the `oxide` ramp - the prairie grain elevator's own red-oxide paint on the same painted timber - and NO NEW RAMP WAS ADDED: corrected for the photographs' light the sample lands five degrees of hue and eight points of saturation from oxide-base. Not `brick`, which is masonry, and not `wood`, which is bare timber.

mustBeRight.feature: a gable end facing the viewer, and a long flank running off it
mustBeRight.detail: The gable rise is 0.735 of the eave height. MEASURED at the LEFT end of work-horse-barn-elevation.jpg, where the eave line is horizontal across 785 px (slope +0.010), which proves the camera sits at eave height and makes the vertical readings there free of foreshortening: ridge 528, eave 692, foundation 915. THE PLAN WIDTH IS NOT MEASURED. It is 1.47 of the eave height, DERIVED from a 12:12 pitch, because no reference in the set gives a gable end free of foreshortening; that is written here rather than left looking like accuracy. The drawn flank is 1.45 eave heights against a real 3.6, shortened so the corral has somewhere to stand - the same decision, for the same reason, as the grain elevator's annex.

mustBeRight.feature: a louvred cupola on the ridge
mustBeRight.why: The ridge vent separates a barn from a house or a machine shed at any scale, and it is the top of the silhouette.
mustBeRight.detail: A small louvred box centred on the ridge over the flank, about 0.43 of the eave height wide, rising about 0.22 of the eave height above the ridge, with its own low pyramid roof and four horizontal louvre bars.

mustBeRight.feature: a run of small white-framed windows along the flank
mustBeRight.detail: Five, evenly spaced: rhythm replacing count (art-bible section 5 rule 3). MEASURED window height 0.233 of the eave height and sill 0.31 of the eave height above the foot, off seven windows on the primary reference. The white frames are the barn's only bright trim and are what stop the flank reading as a blank wall.

mustBeRight.feature: a large sliding door on the gable end
mustBeRight.detail: White-framed, on a visible head track, about 0.4 of the gable-end width, reaching from the foot to a little over half the eave height, with a diagonal ledge brace.

mustBeRight.feature: a peeled-log post-and-rail corral in front of the barn, and a braced gate in it
mustBeRight.why: THIS IS THE FEATURE THAT MAKES THE SUBJECT A RANCH. Without it the render is a barn, which is why every accepted answer names the enclosure or the word ranch.
mustBeRight.detail: Round peeled posts on a regular rhythm with three round rails, in the `wood` ramp from log-rail-fence.jpg, and one gate with a single diagonal brace. Never sawn pickets, never wire, never a stone wall.

mustBeRight.feature: one horse standing inside the corral
mustBeRight.detail: A grey Percheron, from percheron-at-the-barn-wall.jpg. Drawn at 118 px at the withers against the barn's 300 px eave: the eave is about 4.2 m, so 1 m is 71 px and a 1.65 m horse is 117. The animal is at the BUILDING's scale, not at a scale that would read better, which is the only way the barn keeps its measured proportions.

mustBeRight.feature: a grey weathered shingle roof
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED hsl(20,5%,50%), hsl(26,3%,44%) and hsl(0,1%,50%) across three references against `path`'s base at hsl(31,7%,51%), so the roof is drawn in `path` and no grey was added. Not green, not red, not metal.

simplifyAway: the board-and-batten battens and every shingle course beyond an even rhythm
the hay-track hardware, the ladders and the lightning rods
the farm machinery that stands in the yard in every reference
the corral's wire, staples and gate hardware
the horse's dapples, feather and harness
the foundation's stonework, which is one flat band
the Red Ensign that flies over the ranch office in two references: it is a historical flag and drawing it would make the render a claim about a date
neverAdd: any lettering, number or date, in either language
a ranch brand, a company device or a gate sign - an approximated brand is worse than none (art-bible's 'drop, never substitute')
a grain elevator or a silo: that is level 7's landmark and one here would move this level's identity onto another level's subject
a gambrel, hip or round roof - the reference is a straight gable, and a gambrel is the American barn silhouette this one is not
a windmill, a weather vane or a cupola finial
mountains INSIDE this file: the Rocky Mountain front is a parallax layer, and a hero carrying it would put the level's landform on the one render that never repeats
a person, a wagon or a saddle: the rancher is an NPC nobody has placed, and a hero is not where a character goes
notes: The reference set is eight CC BY 2.0 photographs, seven of them from one visit to the Bar U Ranch National Historic Site by one Flickr photographer. LICENCE FIRST, AND IT COST THE BEST FILES: every dedicated barn elevation on Wikimedia Commons - `Bar U Ranch saddle horse barn east side`, `west side`, `work horse barn` - is CC BY-SA 4.0, and the site panoramas are CC BY-SA 3.0, which ADR-0004 excludes for its ShareAlike condition. That is why the measurement leans on a flank view taken in evening light rather than on an orthographic elevation, and why the plan width is a derivation.

subjects.subject: Rolling foothills rangeland: grass ridges with tree bluffs in the folds, a wire fence on wooden posts, cattle grazing and a two-track ranch road.
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the rangeland drawn OVER the foothills, which is the order the level uses. In world coordinates the rangeland tile's top edge is 60 px ABOVE the foothills tile's top edge (world y 880 against 940), so the offset is NEGATIVE: `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'foothills', nearMatch: 'rangeland', nearTop: -60 })`. This is the SECOND negative offset in that table, after prairie-rail-line, and for the same reason: the foreground tile spends its top 250 rows on fence posts and wire that stand UP into the sky. Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 1920) rather than laying them side by side. Neither file answers the subject alone: ridges with no fence and no stock are hills, and a fence with nothing behind it is a fence. THE MOUNTAIN FRONT IS NOT IN THIS COMPOSITE: it lives on layer-20, which is a third tile and is deliberately out of scope, so the answer is a landform these two tiles actually show.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE, and this one has teeth. The foothills tile repeats every 1800 px and the
rangeland every 1920, so neither may carry anything that identifies a place: there is no building of
any kind on either, and the cattle and the fence are types. A verifier who names a province from
these two tiles would be reporting a defect rather than passing.
`the Rockies`, `the Rocky Mountains` and any mountain answer are NOT in this list, and their absence
is deliberate: the mountain front is drawn, on a third tile, and is not in this render. A contract
that accepted it here would reward a memory of the level rather than a reading of the picture.
THE LIST IS WIDE ON THE PLAIN WORDS AND NARROW ON EVERYTHING ELSE, which is the amendment
toronto-trail and rideau-canal-skateway both needed. `farmland` and `prairie` pass because a person
looking at ridges, stock and a fence may honestly say either and would not be wrong about what is
drawn. `a field`, `a park`, `a lawn` and `a golf course` do not: they miss the stock, the fence or
the relief, and those three are the picture.

mustBeRight.feature: rolling grass ridges, one behind another
mustBeRight.detail: Three ridge lines in the `pasture` ramp, each a rolling curve rather than a straight band, with coulees cut down the near faces. Relief is the difference between this subject and the flat farmland of prairie-rail-line, and it is what a verifier is reading.

mustBeRight.feature: dark tree bluffs in the folds of the ridges
mustBeRight.detail: Aspen and spruce clumps in the `pine` ramp, scattered along the ridge feet and in the coulees, as rounded lobes and spires. Never a continuous forest edge.

mustBeRight.feature: a wire fence on wooden posts, running across the whole tile
mustBeRight.why: The post rhythm is what makes movement legible at a horse's speed, and a fence is what tells a viewer this grass is worked rather than wild.
mustBeRight.detail: Posts on an exact divisor of the 1920 px tile so the rhythm does not break at the seam, three wires, and the posts standing UP above the grass horizon into transparent sky.

mustBeRight.feature: cattle grazing
mustBeRight.detail: Hereford - red body, white face, white topline and stockings - from rangeland-cattle-and-wire-fence.jpg. Three per tile, at the grass horizon, small. They are a TYPE and not a herd portrait.

mustBeRight.feature: a two-track ranch road along the ground line
mustBeRight.detail: Two pale wheel tracks in the `felt` ramp with grass between them, on the level's ground polyline. Never a paved road, never a kerb, never a marking.

mustBeRight.feature: yellow-green grass rather than lawn green
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED hsl(75,35%,38%), hsl(83,18%,36%) and hsl(79,40%,29%) across two references. Drawn in the `pasture` ramp, which was ADDED for this level because all three measurements fall OUTSIDE `grass`'s own hue span of 94 to 114 degrees - the same test that kept prairie straw inside `felt` and the museum's glazing inside `ice`.

simplifyAway: every blade, tussock detail and seed head below 12 px
the wire's sag between posts, and the staples
the cattle's ear tags, horns and individual markings
the ruts, gravel and puddles in the two-track
the fence's corner braces and gates
neverAdd: any building at all - a barn, a shed, a house, a windmill or a grain elevator. These are repeating tiles and the level's only non-repeating anchor is `ranch-barn`
a mountain range: it is on layer-20 and this composite is deliberately not asked about it
any lettering, sign or number
a paved road, a power line or a vehicle
a person, and any cultural marker on anything
notes: SCOPED AS A LANDFORM AND NOT A PLACE, which is the whole reason this entry has the shape it does. See `ranch-barn`'s note for what that costs the level.

subjects.subject: A log rail ranch fence with a braced timber gate
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`, the same builder as ranch-barn.
expectedBlindAnswer: a log rail fence and gate
a wooden gate in a rail fence
a gate hung in a rail fence
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. It is a fence and a gate; it names no ranch, no province and no country, and the
level's place-anchor is ranch-barn.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY IS THE GATE. "A fence" alone is a partial answer: the opening, the hung leaf with
its diagonal brace and the two taller posts either side are what make the object a gate, and a first
build failed exactly here - the fence rails ran straight across the opening, so there was nothing to
read as a gap and the leaf read as more fence.

mustBeRight.feature: the fence rails STOP at the gate posts and the opening is clear
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes a gate a gate. Rails carried across the opening make one continuous fence with a decorative diagonal on it.
mustBeRight.detail: Four rails run in from each side and end against the gate posts. Nothing crosses the opening except the gate leaf itself.

mustBeRight.feature: round peeled log rails on squared timber posts, in two different woods
mustBeRight.why: It is the construction the reference shows and it is what separates this from a picket fence or a board fence.
mustBeRight.detail: The rails are ROUND in section - drawn as capsules with a lit top edge and a shaded underside - and weather grey, in the `path` ramp. The posts are SQUARE, brown, in the `wood` ramp, with a capping cut at the top. MEASURED off alberta-foothills/log-rail-fence.jpg: four rails, the lowest about a fifth of the post height above the ground, evenly spaced.

mustBeRight.feature: a hung gate leaf of three rails with one diagonal brace
mustBeRight.why: The brace is what stops a gate sagging and it is the single most recognisable thing about a farm gate.
mustBeRight.detail: Three lighter rails between two stiles, one diagonal running from the bottom of the hinge side to the top of the latch side, and plain dark strap hinges and a latch. The leaf is drawn in a WARMER tone than the fence rails so it reads as a separate object.

mustBeRight.feature: two taller posts framing the opening
mustBeRight.detail: Heavier and darker than the line posts, standing a head above them, capped. They are what the leaf hangs on.

mustBeRight.feature: it stands in pasture, with grass tufts at the posts
mustBeRight.detail: A band of the `pasture` ramp across the bottom with a lit crest and a shaded foot, and small grass tufts where the posts meet it. The file's bottom edge IS the level ground line.

simplifyAway: the grain, the checks and the saw marks in the timber: art-bible section 1 forbids a surface pattern
the through-bolts, the nails and the wire wraps
the board corral and the second fence line behind it in the reference
every post beyond the five drawn: rhythm, not count
neverAdd: a ranch name, a brand, a sign board, a horseshoe device or any lettering in either language. A gateway is exactly where a real ranch puts its name, and this one has none
an arch or an overhead beam between the gate posts: that is a different object - a ranch entrance arch - and no photograph in this repository shows one
barbed wire. Scoped deliberately: a plain wire fence is drawn on alberta-foothills/layer-40-rangeland.svg, which repeats every 1920 px, and the two fences must not be the same fence
a figure, a horse or an animal of any kind: the cattle are their own subject on this level
snow: this level is late summer
notes: alberta-foothills/log-rail-fence.jpg is the PRIMARY reference and it is unusually good for this
purpose: the fence fills the frame in raking light at close range, so the round rails, the square
posts, the two timbers and the spacing are all measurable. It is a GREEN-GRASS exposure and this level
is late summer pasture, so the ground tone is the level's and not the photograph's.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px wide the four rails, the
gate leaf, the diagonal brace, both gate posts and the hinges survive; the 120 px silhouette is a rail
fence with a braced gate in it, which is the subject.

subjects.subject: Three red-bodied white-faced beef cattle standing on rangeland
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE: they are cattle, not a named herd, and the level's place-anchor is ranch-barn.
THE FAILURE TO WATCH FOR IS THE ANIMAL ITSELF. "A llama", "an alpaca", "a horse", "a deer" or "a goat"
is a FAIL and it is the reason this subject has measurements at all: an earlier animal in this project
was read as a llama, and the way a quadruped goes wrong is always the same - the neck gets long, the
head gets high, the body gets shallow and the legs get long. Every mustBeRight entry below is a guard
on one of those four.

mustBeRight.feature: the body is DEEPER than the legs are long
mustBeRight.why: It is the single number that separates cattle from every other farm quadruped at cartoon scale.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on alberta-foothills/rangeland-cattle-and-wire-fence.jpg, on the nearest animals: body depth is about 0.46 of body length and clear leg is about 0.32 of it, so DEPTH : LEG is about 1.4 : 1. The shipped art draws exactly that on all three. Anything under 1 : 1 is a horse or a camelid.

mustBeRight.feature: a SHORT thick neck carrying the head LOW, at or below the line of the back
mustBeRight.why: A raised head on a long neck is what makes a drawn quadruped read as a llama, and it is the specific failure this subject is written against.
mustBeRight.detail: The neck is about a fifth of the body length and it runs forward rather than up. The top of the head sits no higher than the withers. NO upright neck, NO head above the back line.

mustBeRight.feature: a level back with a high rump and a hanging tail with a dark switch
mustBeRight.detail: The top line is flat from the withers to the hip, the hip is the highest point of the body, and the tail hangs straight down from it with a dark tuft at its end. A tail carried out or up belongs to a different animal.

mustBeRight.feature: red body, white face, white underline, white socks over dark hooves
mustBeRight.why: It is the colour pattern of the cattle ALREADY DRAWN on this level's own parallax tile, and a hero in a different pattern would read as a different herd.
mustBeRight.detail: Body in the `brick` ramp, lit along the back; head, neck, belly band and lower legs in `white`; hooves dark. The reference photograph shows solid red animals and the tile draws white-faced ones; the tile wins, because the hero stands 60 px from three of them.

mustBeRight.feature: three animals at three sizes, all facing the same way, on dry pasture
mustBeRight.why: One animal alone has no scale and gives the eye nothing to compare. Three receding sizes read as a herd on open ground.
mustBeRight.detail: Largest nearest the bottom of the frame, smallest highest and furthest, all in profile facing the same direction, overlapping slightly. Dry `pasture` under them with a lit crest and a few grass tufts.

simplifyAway: hair, hide texture and muscle definition: art-bible section 1 forbids a surface pattern
ear tags, brands, tattoos and collars
horns: these are drawn polled, which half of the reference's animals are
the eyelashes, the mouth and the nostrils. Two nostril dots were drawn on a first build and read as a second pair of eyes
the wire fence and the corrals of the reference photograph: the fence is on this level's tile and the gate is its own subject
neverAdd: a brand, an ear tag, a bell, a collar or any lettering in either language
a rider, a herder, a dog or any figure
horns, a hump, a woolly coat or a long neck: each one moves this animal to a different species, and the long neck is the one that has already gone wrong once in this project
a milking udder or a dairy black-and-white pattern: the fact this POI carries is about BEEF, and a Holstein would teach the wrong industry
snow or bare ground: this level is late summer pasture
notes: alberta-foothills/rangeland-cattle-and-wire-fence.jpg is the only reference: a herd on dry grass
behind a wire fence with board corrals beyond. The animals in it are 40 to 90 px long, which settles
PROPORTION and POSTURE and nothing finer, and the drawing does not pretend past that.
THE COLOUR COMES FROM THE TILE AND NOT FROM THE PHOTOGRAPH, which is the one place this subject
deliberately departs from its reference. The photograph shows solid red animals;
alberta-foothills/layer-40-rangeland.svg already draws three red-bodied white-faced ones, and a hero
standing in front of them in a different pattern would read as a different kind of animal rather than
as the near view of the same herd. Both patterns are common on this rangeland.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw the nearest animal below 200 px long anywhere the player is meant to read
the species. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 280 px wide all three animals, their white
faces, their socks and their tails are legible; at 180 px the smallest becomes a shape and the two
nearest still read.

subjects.subject: An oil pump jack on a gravel lease in foothills pasture: a red horsehead on a pale grey walking beam balanced on an A-frame Samson post, pitman arms down to a crank with red counterweights on a black gear reducer, and the bridle hanging from the horsehead to a wellhead
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`, the same builder as ranch-barn and beef-cattle.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: A TYPE AND NOT A PLACE, on the test ranch-barn and grain-elevator pass: a beam pump is a standard machine
on oil fields across North America and beyond, and nothing drawn says which province. `Alberta` is NOT in the
accepted list and the gate MUST NOT reward it; the level's page-101 fact is carried by the card, not by the
picture. WHAT IT MUST CARRY IS THE MECHANISM: the beam on its fulcrum, the curved head over the well and the
counterweighted crank. "A drilling rig" or "an oil derrick" is a FAIL - a derrick is a tower over a hole
being drilled and a producing well has none - and "a crane", "a see-saw" or "a hammer" are the failures a
wrong silhouette produces.

mustBeRight.feature: a walking beam balanced on an A-frame Samson post, longer in front of the post than behind it
mustBeRight.why: The lever is the machine. Without the fulcrum between the two ends it is a crane or a boom.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on alberta-foothills/pump-jack-dusk-in-snow.jpg (1600x1067), the only clean side profile in the set: a dark silhouette against the sky, thresholded row by row. EVERY FIGURE IS IN S, the height of the saddle bearing above the skid (370 px), because the beam's tilt changes every other height with the phase of the stroke. Saddle to horsehead face 247 px, 0.70 S along an 18-degree beam; saddle to the beam's rear end 187 px, 0.53 S. Checked on pump-jack-side-elevation.jpg, which is a three-quarter view and so a check and not a measurement: 0.66 S and 0.54 S. Drawn at S = 300: face 222 px from the pivot, 0.74 S; rear arm 160 px, 0.53 S. The beam is drawn tilted 6 degrees, horsehead up; the reference's 18 is a phase and not a proportion.

mustBeRight.feature: a red horsehead with a curved face at the well end of the beam
mustBeRight.why: The single most recognisable part and the top of the silhouette.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED 230 px tall on the dusk profile, 0.62 S, sitting about a third above the beam and two thirds below it; drawn 186 px, 0.62 S. The face is an arc centred on the saddle bearing - which is how the machine keeps the bridle vertical - so the wellhead stands directly under the face at the pivot's own height. A SOLID BLOCK WITH A FLAT BACK, deepest where the beam enters: a first build tapered it to two points and at 390 px it read as a leaf. Red sampled on pump-jack-foothills-county.jpg, lit hsl(7,96%,65%) and in shade hsl(5,96%,26%); drawn in `serge` (base hsl(4,65%,47%)), the palette's nearest red by hue - `flag-red` sits at 358 and `oxide` is the barn's red-oxide paint.

mustBeRight.feature: pitman arms from the beam's rear end down to a counterweighted crank on a gear reducer
mustBeRight.why: It is the drive, and the counterweight is the second-largest shape in the silhouette.
mustBeRight.detail: Pitman 0.49 S on the dusk profile, from the beam to the crank pin at row 790; drawn 155 px, 0.52 S. The reducer is a black housing on a pedestal at the back of the skid, its output shaft 0.24 S above the skid top measured and 0.27 S drawn. The counterweights are sector-shaped plates on the crank arm, red, as on pump-jack-foothills-county.jpg; the crank is drawn pointing up and back, a phase in which the grassland units in pump-jacks-on-grassland.jpg show theirs.

mustBeRight.feature: a bridle and polished rod hanging from the horsehead to a small wellhead on the ground
mustBeRight.why: It connects the machine to the well, and it is what separates a pump jack from any other pivoting beam.
mustBeRight.detail: Wire rope over the face, a carrier bar, a bright polished rod, and a short stack of stuffing box, valve body with two side valves, and flange, standing clear of the skid in front of it as on the dusk profile.

mustBeRight.feature: a motor and belt guard behind the reducer on one long steel skid, on a gravel lease
mustBeRight.detail: Motor rear to wellhead 1.69 S on the dusk profile; drawn 525 px, 1.75 S. The skid runs from behind the motor to the Samson post's front leg and stops there.

mustBeRight.feature: pale grey steel, a red horsehead, red counterweights, a red ladder and a black reducer
mustBeRight.why: It is the scheme of the one Alberta unit photographed in true colour, and it keeps the machine off the near-black of the dusk frame, which is a colour grade and not paint.
mustBeRight.detail: Sampled on pump-jack-foothills-county.jpg: Samson post lit hsl(231,22%,87%), beam in shade hsl(195,15%,39%), reducer hsl(180,15%,7%). Drawn with `white-shade` as the steel's base, `white-base` lit and `slate-light` in shade - the palette has no grey steel ramp and these are its nearest tones - and the `hide` ramp for the reducer. A DEPARTURE, STATED: the Foothills County unit is a rear-fulcrum machine - its Samson post stands at the rear end of the beam and its cranks sit under the horsehead - while the other three references are conventional units with the post mid-beam and the cranks at the rear. The geometry drawn is the conventional one, measured on the other Alberta unit, and the Foothills unit supplies paint only. Averaging the two geometries would draw a machine nobody built.

simplifyAway: the chain-link fence, the lease sign, the aerial and the electrical cabinet round the Foothills County unit
the ladder cage and the walkway platforms
bolts, pins under 12 px, the brake lever and the stroke-adjust holes in the crank arm
the lightening holes in the dusk unit's horsehead: the Foothills unit's head is solid, and a hole pattern is a maker's
the hay bales round the lease, and the flow lines and small tanks on the grassland pad
neverAdd: the maker's name on the walking beam, a lease sign, a well licence plate, an operator's logo or any lettering in either language
a derrick, a drilling mast or a flare stack: a producing well has none, and each is a different object
oil on the ground, a spill, a gusher or oil drums
a worker, a truck or any figure
a second pump jack on this hero: one machine is the point of interest, and a row of them is an oil field
snow: this level is late summer
notes: alberta-foothills/pump-jack-dusk-in-snow.jpg (CC BY 2.0) is the GEOMETRY reference and nothing else: a heavy
teal-and-orange grade, never sampled for colour. alberta-foothills/pump-jack-foothills-county.jpg (CC BY 3.0) is
the COLOUR reference and the Alberta context; its geometry is a different class of unit (mustBeRight, last
entry). pump-jack-side-elevation.jpg (public domain, Florida) and pump-jacks-on-grassland.jpg (public domain,
North Dakota) are mechanism checks, and neither is drawn as a place.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 165 px wide (25 per cent) the horsehead, the
beam on its A-frame, the counterweight and the wellhead all survive; the 120 px silhouette is a tilted beam on
a tripod with a curved head over a well, which is the subject.

subjects.subject: A saddled bay ranch horse walking, seen from its near side: a quarter-horse type under a tan western saddle with a horn
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x with `singleSource()`. It is the behind layer of the Alberta foothills ride (ADR-0031): the engine draws the player IN FRONT of this file, astride, so this render shows the horse saddled and riderless. That is deliberate, and it is the park car's reason: the rider is the rig's (`horse/*` in rig-contract.json), and a ride subject built with a pose would fall under the hand-off's mounted-subject rules, which require `{mode}` equipment frames that a ride by definition does not have. `verify-art` reports `horse` as a posed mode with no subject, and that report is the true statement.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: A TYPE AND NOT A PLACE, on the test pump-jack and ranch-barn pass: a saddled quarter horse is the working
horse of ranches across western North America, and nothing drawn says which province. `Alberta` is NOT in
the accepted list and the gate MUST NOT reward it.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY IS THE ANIMAL AND THE SADDLE. `A pony`, `a donkey` or `a mule` are near misses and fail:
the proportions below are measured so that it is none of them. `A llama`, `a camel`, `a deer`, `a cow` or
`a dog` are the failures a wrong silhouette produces, and they are the reason the neck, the head carriage
and the leg length are guarded. An answer that names the horse and not the saddle is a partial answer:
the horn, the skirt and the stirrup are what make it a horse somebody rides.

mustBeRight.feature: a deep round barrel, and legs below it no longer than the barrel is deep
mustBeRight.why: Leg length against body depth is the number that separates a horse from a deer, a llama or a foal at cartoon scale; the way a drawn quadruped goes wrong is always long legs under a shallow body.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED 2026-09-14 on alberta-foothills/quarter-horse-side-elevation.jpg, a broadside view, against W = the withers height above the hooves: barrel depth at the girth 0.51 W, clear leg from the girth to the ground 0.49 W, body length from the point of the shoulder to the point of the buttock 1.08 W. Drawn at W = 315 px: barrel 171 px, clear leg 144 px, body length 355 px. The croup stands level with the withers, as a quarter horse's does.

mustBeRight.feature: a short thick neck carried forward, with the head angled down and the poll barely above the withers
mustBeRight.why: An upright neck and a raised head are what made this level's first drawn horse read as a llama (alberta-foothills-level.md section 6.3). They are guarded by number here.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on the same photograph: the poll 0.54 W ahead of the withers and 0.20 W above them, the muzzle 0.75 W ahead and 0.17 W below. Drawn: the poll 171 px ahead and 59 px above, the muzzle 250 px ahead and 55 px below. The head is drawn about ten percent larger than measured, the one cartoon departure, so the eye, ears and nostril survive at 390 px.

mustBeRight.feature: a brown coat with a black mane, a black tail and black lower legs: a bay
mustBeRight.why: Bay is the commonest horse colour and the one that says horse at a glance; the black points also keep the four legs legible against the pasture trail.
mustBeRight.detail: Coat in the `leather` ramp, mane, tail, knees and hocks down in `hair-black`, hooves in `hide`. NOT MEASURED from one photograph and said so: the proportion reference is a buckskin and the saddle reference is a dark bay in hard backlight. Bay was chosen over both so that the ride separates from the grey Percheron in the barn corral and from the red white-faced cattle on this level.

mustBeRight.feature: a western saddle with a horn, a square skirt, a fender, a cinch and a stirrup, on a pad
mustBeRight.why: The horn and the square skirt are what make the saddle western and the horse a ranch horse; an English saddle is a small flap with no horn.
mustBeRight.detail: From alberta-foothills/cow-horse-under-western-saddle.jpg: the horn stands over the withers, the seat dips behind it and rises to the cantle, the skirt is square with rounded corners, the fender hangs under the rider's thigh, the cinch runs down behind the elbow, and the stirrup hangs at the belly line with the rider's boot in it. Saddle leather in `wood` so it reads as a tan saddle on a brown horse; a plain `felt` pad shows under the skirt.

mustBeRight.feature: a walking stride: the near foreleg reaching forward, the near hind leg trailing, the far pair under the body
mustBeRight.why: The ride's art is one still image (ADR-0031) that travels with the player, so the stance has to read as walking by itself; four square legs sliding along read as a statue on wheels.
mustBeRight.detail: From alberta-foothills/horse-walking-muybridge-plate-574.jpg, frame 2 of the top row: three feet on the ground, the near fore planted ahead of the body and the near hind behind it, the far pair close under the belly. Far legs one tone darker, which is how depth reads without an outline.

mustBeRight.feature: a bridle with one rein running back to the saddle horn
mustBeRight.why: It is what connects the rider's hands to the horse; without it the player is sitting on the animal rather than riding it.
mustBeRight.detail: A plain leather headstall, browband and noseband, a small brass bit ring at the corner of the mouth, and one rein curving back along the neck to the horn, where the rider's fists hold it.

simplifyAway: the coat's dapples, whorls and muscle definition: three flat tones
the saddle's tooling, conchos, latigo, rigging rings and back cinch
the rope, and everything the reference rider carries
the far rein, the throatlatch and the curb strap
the chestnuts, the ergots and the shoes
neverAdd: a brand, a number, a name or lettering of any kind, including a ranch brand on the hip
a patterned saddle blanket: no invented pattern, and a blanket in any nation's style would be a depiction of that nation's design

subjects.subject: Canada Place, Vancouver: the cruise-ship terminal and convention centre, five white fabric sails on masts over a long two-level pier building standing on piles in Burrard Inlet.
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`. The file is 1000 x 800 and its bottom 280 rows are deliberately empty, so the rasterised subject is a building floating above the foot of the frame; that is not a defect and the reason is in the file's own title.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT IS ALLOWED TO DEMAND A PLACE NAME, and it is the only render in this level that may. It
is a single non-repeating POI hero drawing one specific building whose five white fabric sails on a
long low pier are shared by nothing else this game will ever draw. A verifier who cannot place it is
reporting a defect in the drawing. `vancouver-seawall` is two repeating tiles and is asked for a
waterfront path and never for a city, so Vancouver as a place rests on this render alone.
AND THE BUILDING'S OWN NAME IS NOT IN THE LIST, WHICH IS A DEFECT IN THE HARNESS AND NOT IN THE ART.
`leakTokens` takes every word of four letters or more out of `id` and `expectedBlindAnswer` and
refuses any handed-over text that contains one; the briefing the hand-off writes asks the identifier
to name a real, named p-l-a-c-e or thing. The building's name contains that noun, so writing it here
would turn make verify-art red on a hand-off that leaks nothing - and the subject id is `five-sails`
rather than the building's name for exactly the same reason.
