which is what the building is popularly called and is the count its own architecture is named for.
The residual risk is stated plainly: a verifier who writes the building's name AND NOTHING ELSE is
scored a miss while being exactly right. The fix is one line and is routed rather than worked around:
reword the briefing to ask for `a real, named building or landmark`. This entry is amended the day
that lands. `pier-21`'s note stated this rule first; this is its most expensive instance.

mustBeRight.feature: exactly five white fabric sails
mustBeRight.why: The count is the identification. Art-bible section 5 rule 3 lets a repeated detail's number differ from the reference; here the number IS the feature, and the building is popularly called by it.
mustBeRight.detail: Five sharp peaks in a row on one continuous white fabric mass, in the `white` ramp. Four reads as a marquee and six as a circus tent; neither is this building.

mustBeRight.feature: asymmetric sails: a steep concave rise on the left to a sharp peak, then a long shallow sweep down to the right
mustBeRight.why: This is the whole shape. The first build drew five symmetric cones and they read as tents.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on five-sails-close.jpg: between the first and second masts the fabric bottoms out at y 700 against peaks at y 300 and a deck at y 1100 - 42 per cent of the drop, NOT the whole of it. mustBeRight.feature: the sails stand on a long, low, two-level white building
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED against H = the sail peak to the waterline, in one column at the near end of canada-place-from-the-west.jpg: sails 0.384 H, the deck-edge zone 0.070 H, the two-level block 0.411 H, the piles and their shadow 0.135 H, and the mast spacing 0.384 H, so a sail is as wide as it is tall. The block is longer than the sail row and reads as a pier, not a hall.

mustBeRight.feature: the building stands on piles over open water
mustBeRight.why: It is a pier. A version of this building sitting on a shore is a conference centre and not this one.
mustBeRight.detail: A dark under-deck shadow, a rhythm of piles below it, and water at the foot. Its base does not touch the bottom of the frame.

mustBeRight.feature: stay cables fanning down to the right of every mast
mustBeRight.detail: Two or three straight lines from each mast head down to the deck, in the `slate` ramp, from sail-masts-and-rigging.jpg. They are the one dark element on a white building and are what stops the sail row reading as a paper cut-out.

mustBeRight.feature: the National Flag of Canada on the promenade
mustBeRight.detail: ONE flag on a short pole at deck level, where the primary reference shows several. Drawn 46 px wide at design resolution; the art bible's floor is 40, below which a flag stops being a flag. The leaf is a bold five-lobe silhouette, not an eleven-point outline.

mustBeRight.feature: a glazed colonnade under the promenade deck
mustBeRight.detail: White columns on a regular bay with the recess dark behind them, in `slate` and `ice`. The under-deck is in its own shadow in every reference, and drawing it light makes the pier read as a cruise ship.

the second and third rows of sails behind the first, which produce eight to ten apparent peaks from most angles

subjects.subject: A paved waterfront path along a low sea wall with a white balustrade, open salt water beyond it, benches, lamp standards, conifers and gulls.
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the seawall drawn OVER the inlet, which is the order the level uses. The seawall tile's top edge is 40 px BELOW the inlet tile's top edge (world y 900 against 860): `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'inlet', nearMatch: 'seawall', nearTop: 40 })`. Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 1920). THE SEAM CLOSES HERE, unlike toronto-trail and winnipeg-riverwalk: the inlet tile is opaque from its own top edge and runs to composite y 300, and the seawall tile is opaque from composite y 290, so the two overlap by 10 px and no matte shows between them. The 40 px above the inlet's top edge carries the cedar tops, the lamp heads and the gulls.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. Both tiles repeat - 1800 and 1920 - so neither may carry a recognisable building:
the far shore is plain masses and conifers, the two gantry cranes are types, and the ferry and the
bulk carrier are types. A verifier who names a city from these two tiles would be reporting a defect.
EVERY ACCEPTED PHRASE NAMES THE WATER, and that is the line this list draws rather than a preference.
Half of this composite is open salt water and the wall exists because of it, so `a promenade`, `a
park path`, `a paved walkway` and `a boardwalk` alone do NOT pass. Two of those are accepted answers
of `winnipeg-riverwalk`, whose picture is a stone parapet with no open water in it, and a list that
accepted both would stop being able to tell the two subjects apart - which is the reason that entry
gives for refusing `a boardwalk`.
WHERE VANCOUVER ACTUALLY COMES FROM: `five-sails`, a separate non-repeating POI hero. The seawall is
where the player travels; the pier is what says which city.

mustBeRight.feature: open salt water in flat tones, filling the upper half
mustBeRight.detail: Three flat `water` tones and straight ripple bars, never a gradient and never a blur (ADR-0011). MEASURED hsl(204,29%,22%) on canada-place-and-the-north-shore.jpg against water-shade's hsl(210,65%,29%).

mustBeRight.feature: a white balustrade of turned balusters between heavier piers
mustBeRight.why: It is the one piece of furniture that says SEA WALL rather than park railing, and it is what the reference actually has.
mustBeRight.detail: A continuous run of short white balusters under a coping rail, with a broader pier every 208 px, from seawall-path-and-harbour.jpg. Never a steel guardrail, never glass.

mustBeRight.feature: a paved path along the near side of the wall
mustBeRight.detail: Flat `path` tones with joint lines on a rhythm. It is the surface the player travels on and must read as paving rather than as sand or grass.

mustBeRight.feature: a lawn verge with benches on it
mustBeRight.detail: A strip of `grass` between the balustrade and the paving, with timber-slat benches on steel legs. `grass` and not level 8's `pasture`: a mown seaside park lawn is the same material as the lawn on Parliament Hill.

mustBeRight.detail: Two western red cedars per tile as stacked dark lobed tiers, and twin-globe lamp standards on a 470 px rhythm. Both stand ABOVE the tile's opaque line into transparent sky, which is why the tile is 430 px tall.

mustBeRight.feature: gulls
mustBeRight.detail: Flat white double-arc shapes in the air, three to seven per tile. They are the one thing that puts the picture at the sea rather than at a lake.

mustBeRight.feature: people with no cultural marker of any kind

the wave texture, foam and reflections on the water

subjects.subject: Moored sailing boats in a harbour marina
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`, the same builder as five-sails.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. They are boats, not a named marina or a named vessel, and this level’s
place-anchor is five-sails and nothing else.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY IS THAT THEY ARE SAILING BOATS AT REST. "A ship", "a ferry" or "a fishing boat" is
a partial answer; "a regatta" or "boats under sail" is a FAIL, because nothing here carries a sail.
The bare masts with their booms are the whole point: a moored boat has its sails off.

mustBeRight.feature: THREE boats at three sizes and three distances, not one
mustBeRight.why: One boat is a boat; three at different distances is a marina, which is what the fact this POI carries is about.
mustBeRight.detail: The nearest lowest in the frame and largest, the other two smaller and higher, overlapping. All lying the same way, none under way, no wake and no bow wave.

mustBeRight.feature: white hulls with a dark boot stripe, and a sheer that rises to the bow
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED from the marina in vancouver/coal-harbour-and-the-north-shore.jpg, where forty-odd hulls fill the middle distance and every one of them is white: freeboard is about 0.16 of hull length and the bow is about 0.15 of the freeboard higher than the stern. The boot stripe is a narrow dark band at the waterline and is the only colour on the hull.

mustBeRight.feature: one mast and one boom on each, bare
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes them sailing boats. A mastless hull is a motor launch and the reference marina is mostly sailing boats.
mustBeRight.detail: A single vertical mast forward of amidships, tapering, with a horizontal boom at its foot running aft. No shrouds, no stays, no rigging lines: at this size a 3 px line is noise, and art-bible section 1 sets the floor at 12 px.

mustBeRight.feature: a low cabin trunk with two dark windows
mustBeRight.detail: A rounded box on the deck, about a third of the hull length, with two small dark lights in its side. It is what separates a yacht from an open dinghy.

mustBeRight.feature: open water under them and the stone edge of the seawall walk across the bottom
mustBeRight.why: The boats have to be IN something. The seawall edge is also what ties the hero to the ground the player is standing on.
mustBeRight.detail: Three flat `water` tones, darkest nearest the camera where the wall shades it, with straight lit ripple bars, two yellow mooring buoys, and a band of `limestone` paving at the bottom of the file. The file’s bottom edge IS the level ground line.

simplifyAway: shrouds, stays, halyards, lifelines and every other line
sail covers, winches, cleats, fenders and rails below 12 px
the floating docks and finger piers: a first build drew one across the front and the nearest hull read as sitting ON it
the forty other boats in the reference photograph
the flower bed the reference is actually a photograph of: it is in sharp focus and the marina is the blurred background, and the marina is the subject here
neverAdd: a boat name, a sail number, a class insignia, a burgee, an ensign or any lettering in either language
a sail set, a spinnaker, a wake or a bow wave: these boats are moored

a totem pole or an inuksuk, in any form, including background, silhouette, icon and loading art. docs/content-review.md 5.2 and 5.4, and it is on BOTH of this level’s original subjects for the same reason: this level is the single most likely place in this game for those rules to be broken by accident

the Lions Gate Bridge or Canada Place in the same frame. Scoped deliberately: the five sails are REQUIRED on five-sails and the bridge is the recorded fallback anchor, and neither may appear on a subject judged in the same hand-off
a figure on any deck
notes: vancouver/coal-harbour-and-the-north-shore.jpg is the PRIMARY reference and it is an odd one: the
photograph is OF a flower bed, sharply focused, and the marina behind it is soft. That is exactly what
makes it useful here - it gives the massing, the colour and the density of forty hulls at a glance and
no detail at all, which is the level of description this drawing wants.
seawall-path-and-harbour.jpg gives the same marina from further away with the seawall in front of it,
which is the arrangement this hero draws.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px wide all three hulls,
their boot stripes, all three masts and booms and both buoys survive; the 120 px silhouette is three
overlapping hulls under three bare masts.

subjects.subject: A bulk carrier lying in a harbour
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE AND STRICTLY SO: a real ship carries a name, a port of registry, draught marks, a
funnel device and an ensign, and every one of those names an owner or a country. This one carries none.
The level’s place-anchor is five-sails.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY IS CARGO. "A cruise ship", "a ferry", "a warship" or "a liner" is a FAIL: the hatch
covers down an open weather deck, the deck cranes and the superstructure pushed right aft are what make
this a working cargo ship, and a passenger vessel has none of them.

mustBeRight.feature: the superstructure is right AFT, over the stern, and there is nothing else above the deck line
mustBeRight.why: It is the single strongest silhouette cue for a cargo ship and the thing a passenger ship never does.
mustBeRight.detail: A white block of three or four storeys standing at one end of the hull with a funnel above it, and the whole of the rest of the ship flat. MEASURED loosely off the ships in the background of vancouver/canada-place-and-the-north-shore.jpg: the superstructure is about a fifth of the ship’s length.

mustBeRight.feature: a line of raised hatch covers along the weather deck
mustBeRight.why: It is what says the cargo is IN the ship rather than stacked on it, and it is what separates this from the container car on another level of this game.
mustBeRight.detail: Four low rectangles on the deck at an even period, lit along the top edge. Rhythm, not count.

mustBeRight.feature: pedestal deck cranes with their jibs stowed
mustBeRight.detail: Four posts standing between the hatches, each with a straight jib angled up and aft. They are the second-strongest cue and they are what makes the ship read as self-loading rather than as a barge.

mustBeRight.feature: a long low dark hull with a black boot stripe and a flared bow
mustBeRight.detail: Hull length about six times its visible depth, the deck line straight, the bow flaring out to a rounded stem at one end and the stern rounded at the other. Dark red in the `oxide` ramp with the boot stripe at the waterline.

mustBeRight.feature: it lies in open water, at rest, with the seawall edge across the bottom of the frame
mustBeRight.detail: Flat `water` tones with lit ripple bars, darkest nearest the camera, and a band of `limestone` paving at the file’s bottom edge, which IS the level ground line. NO wake, NO bow wave, NO smoke.

simplifyAway: the name, the port of registry, the draught marks, the load line and the IMO number
accommodation ladders, lifeboats, davits, railings and mooring lines
the anchor, the hawse pipes and the bulbous bow below the waterline
the containers: this ship carries bulk, and a container stack would make it the same object as prairie-rail’s container-car
neverAdd: a name, a funnel device, a house flag, an ensign, a wordmark or any lettering in either language
a container stack, a car deck, a passenger promenade or a cruise ship’s tiered balconies
smoke from the funnel: it would put the ship under way and would be an effect with no plain path (ADR-0011)

a totem pole or an inuksuk, in any form, including background, silhouette, icon and loading art. docs/content-review.md 5.2 and 5.4, and it is on BOTH of this level’s original subjects for the same reason: this level is the single most likely place in this game for those rules to be broken by accident
Canada Place’s five sails in the same frame, for the reason marina-boats gives
notes: THE REFERENCES FOR THIS SUBJECT ARE DISTANT AND THAT IS STATED RATHER THAN DRESSED UP. The ships in
vancouver/canada-place-and-the-north-shore.jpg and coal-harbour-and-the-north-shore.jpg are in the far
background at a few hundred pixels; what they settle is the ARRANGEMENT - aft superstructure, flat
deck, cranes - which is the level of detail a 390 px phone frame shows, and nothing finer is claimed.

for the trading-nation fact, and a container ship here would be the same object twice in one game. The
Port of Vancouver moves both; the hatch covers and cranes are the half that is not drawn anywhere else.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px wide the aft block, the
funnel, all four cranes, the hatch covers and the boot stripe survive; the 120 px silhouette is a long
low hull with a tall block at one end and four masts along it.

subjects.renderRecipe: BUILT FROM THE RIG CONTRACT, so `renders` is empty on purpose: scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs composes this subject from assets/style/rig-contract.json (its MOUNTS table names the mode, the state and the frame), and the part sources are listed in `notes` as documentation rather than as input. What the builder does, and why: A MOUNTED CHARACTER IS NEVER JUDGED FROM ONE FILE AND NEVER AT REST. Build the player composite exactly as the `player` subject's recipe says - parts from assets/style/rig-contract.json in `z` order, costume=parka, any skin, hair and head covering - and then two things that recipe does not do. Pin the `{mode}` brace to `skate` - the level's locomotion mode, which is not a slot - which is what makes the two skates resolve. And pose it: take `skate/walk` from `states`, lerp the per-part `[dx, dy, rotationDegrees]` on `t`, and render MID-MOTION at t=0, not the rest pose. A rest-pose render of a mounted character is the render that passed four rounds of review while the defect was still on the phone. A pose leaves character space in every direction, so the canvas is not a fixed anchor: the builder measures one window from the rotated part windows of all four mounted poses, adds a 4 px margin, and frames all four in it, so their sole lines and crowns sit on the same rows. See assets/style/rig-contract.md 11.4. JUDGE IT AT 390 px OVER THE OTTAWA CANAL (src/svg/ottawa/layer-50-canalwall.svg above src/svg/ottawa/layer-60-ice.svg, ice at world 1280, the figure’s sole line on 1280), which is where a player sees it; a cue that is 2 px on a phone is not a cue.

toe picks
blade sharpening hollow

subjects.subject: Peggy's Point Lighthouse, Nova Scotia: a short, heavily tapered, octagonal white concrete tower carrying a red lantern room with a red conical roof and a ball finial, on a wide white gallery deck with a dark railing, standing on bare granite.
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`. The file is 480 x 900; the tower occupies rows 26 to 866 and the 34 rows below it carry only the ground-contact AO, so the subject sits almost on the foot of the frame. There is NO deliberate empty band here, unlike five-sails: this building stands on rock and not on piles, so it is drawn tight to its own base and the barrens tile passes behind it rather than in front.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THE KIND OF THING PASSES; THE PLACE NAME IS A BONUS. Amended 2026-09-17, and this subject is the
one that proved the point: a blind verifier answered `a lighthouse`, which is what the drawing
shows, and the contract scored it a miss. `a lighthouse` now PASSES. The place names stay accepted
and naming it is strong positive evidence. The note below already predicted this outcome and called
the honest fix a second cited POI rather than a longer answer list; that finding STANDS and is now
a matter for the contract owner, because a passing verdict here no longer establishes the place.
IT IS STILL THE ONLY RENDER ON THIS LEVEL THAT COULD CARRY A PLACE NAME AT ALL.
It is a single non-repeating POI hero drawing one specific building. `peggys-cove-barrens` is two
repeating tiles and is asked for a rocky fishing harbour and never for a place, so this level's PLACE
rests on this render alone - the same arrangement as five-sails on the vancouver level.
AND IT IS A HARDER ASK THAN FIVE-SAILS, WHICH IS STATED RATHER THAN HOPED AWAY. Canada Place is one
building of its kind in the world; there are several hundred lighthouses in Nova Scotia alone, and a
verifier who answers `a lighthouse on the Atlantic coast` is not wrong, only unhelpful. IT USED TO BE
SCORED A MISS FOR THAT, AND THAT WAS THE DEFECT: `unhelpful` is a finding about the level, and the
contract turned it into a failure of the drawing. The claim this entry makes is that the PROPORTIONS
identify it: a tower 2.37 base widths tall whose top three tenths are red is a specific, measured,
unusual shape, and it is the most photographed lighthouse in Canada. That claim is now TESTED rather
than ENFORCED - a verifier who volunteers the place has confirmed it, and one who does not has not
refuted the drawing. THE PREDICTION IN THE LINE BELOW HAS COME TRUE, and it is the open finding this
amendment hands to the contract owner: a real blind pass returned only the type, so this level has no
place anchor, and the honest fix is a second cited POI and not a longer answer list.
ON THE LEAK TOKENS: `lighthouse` is now an accepted answer, so it is a leak token like every other
word of four letters or more here, and the hand-off refuses any text it hands over that contains one.
`light` was already a token by way of this subject's id, so nothing new is forbidden to the briefing;
checked against the shipped briefing, the Makefile and the CLI on 2026-09-17, with no collision.

mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on refs/peggys-cove/lighthouse-elevation.jpg in the column through the tower's axis: the finial tip is at y150, the foot at y690, so H = 540; the foot spans x362..x588 = 226 px. 540/226 = 2.39. Drawn at H = 840 with a base of 354: 2.37. Art-bible section 5 rule 1 allows plus or minus ten per cent and this ratio should not use it.

mustBeRight.feature: the red top is three tenths of the whole height
mustBeRight.why: The second identifying proportion. A small red cap on a tall white tower is a different building.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on the same file: the red assembly runs from the finial tip at y150 to the underside of the gallery deck at y314 = 164 px of 540 = 0.304. Drawn 26 to 281 of 840 = 0.304. mustBeRight.feature: the gallery deck oversails the shaft by half again, on a CONCAVE corbel
mustBeRight.why: The flare is what makes the silhouette read as a lighthouse at 120 px rather than as a chimney.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED: the deck is 210 px wide against a shaft top of 142 px = 1.48x, at H = 540. Drawn 327 against 221 = 1.48x. The corbel between them is a concave sweep over 0.039 H, not a straight chamfer and not a bracketed cornice.

mustBeRight.feature: a dark railing standing on the deck, in front of the lantern's solid panel
mustBeRight.detail: Seven posts and two horizontal rails in the `slate` ramp, spanning the full width of the deck, so the two outermost posts stand against open sky beyond the lantern. That overhang is what the reference shows and it is what stops the deck reading as a plain slab.

mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED: 142 px at the top of the shaft to 226 px at the foot = 1.59x over 0.657 H. Drawn 221 to 354 = 1.60x. subjects.subject: A small fishing harbour of board-and-batten stores on spruce piles seen across sheltered water from a foreground of bare, rounded, jointed granite with grass in its cracks and tide pools in its hollows.
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the barrens drawn OVER the cove, which is the order the level uses. The barrens tile's top edge is 160 px BELOW the cove tile's top edge (world y 1000 against 840): `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'cove', nearMatch: 'barrens', nearTop: 160 })`. Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1760 and 1920). The composite is 440 rows: the cove occupies 0..270 and the barrens 160..440, overlapping by 110. THE SEAM CLOSES TO THE PIXEL and the number is measured rather than asserted: the cove tile's last row is world 1110 and the barrens tile's FIRST FULLY OPAQUE row is world 1110 (its own row 110), so nothing shows between them at any x. Above that line the barrens carries rock crest against transparency from world 1024 down, and the cove's wharf, stores and water are MEANT to show between the crests: that is the view from the barrens and it is why the two tiles are one subject. AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS ENTRY SAID 80 AND THE LEVEL DOCUMENT SAID 120, AND BOTH WERE WRONG. The tiles were redrawn on 2026-09-13 after the composite showed the rock walling off the harbour; the cove tile went from 280 rows at world 880 to 270 at world 840 and the barrens from 320 at world 960 to 280 at world 1000, and 160 is the measured offset between what shipped. Anything reading this file for a number should take it from here and from content/levels/peggys-cove.json, which now agree.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. Both tiles repeat - 1760 and 1920 - so neither may carry a recognisable building:
every store, boat, wharf and headland on them is a TYPE, and there is no lettering, hull name, number
or livery anywhere. A verifier who names a place from these two tiles is reporting a defect.
EVERY ACCEPTED PHRASE NAMES EITHER THE FISHING OR THE ROCK, and that is a line this list draws rather
than a preference. `a working waterfront`, `a harbour boardwalk` and `a wharf promenade` are accepted
answers of halifax-quayside, whose picture is a timber boardwalk in front of a town, and a list that
accepted them here would stop being able to tell the two subjects apart. This one has bare rock across
its whole foreground and sheds standing on piles over open water, and Halifax has neither.
WHERE THE PLACE ACTUALLY COMES FROM: `peggys-cove-light`, a separate non-repeating POI hero.
THREE PHRASES WERE REMOVED FROM THIS LIST BY THE GATE AND NOT BY TASTE. `fish sheds over the
water`, `a small harbour with fishing boats` and `a rocky shore with a fishing harbour` each
contributed an ordinary English word - over, small, with - that the hand-off's own briefing
already contains, and `leakTokens` refuses any handed-over text holding a token from an accepted
answer. pier-21's note states the rule and five-sails is its most expensive instance; this is the
cheapest, because every phrase dropped has a synonym in the list that survives.

mustBeRight.feature: bare, rounded, jointed granite across the whole foreground, in near-neutral warm grey
mustBeRight.why: It is the surface the player walks on and it is the one landform that says this coast rather than any coast.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on refs/peggys-cove/granite-barrens-and-sea.jpg: 520x60 at (420,470) has median hsl(40,23%,71%) and 300x40 at (620,500) has median hsl(33,17%,50%), against path-light's hsl(42,6%,67%) and path-base's hsl(36,6%,52%). Two flat-light references of the same rock read LESS saturated than the ramp, so the ramp sits inside the bracket and no granite ramp was added. Rounded whaleback masses divided by long curving joints, never angular scree and never a cliff.

mustBeRight.feature: grass ONLY in the joints
mustBeRight.why: Grass spread over the rock turns barrens into a meadow, and that was the first build's defect.
mustBeRight.detail: Nine broken runs of low tufts per tile, each following a joint line and tapering at both ends, in `grass-shade` with a little `grass-base` on top. Never a patch on open rock, never a lawn.

mustBeRight.feature: tide pools set into the rock, with an irregular rim
mustBeRight.why: At the low preset this level keeps two layers and they are the sky and this one, so without the pools a coastal level would show no water at the tier most phones get.
mustBeRight.detail: Two per tile, irregular rings rather than ellipses, `path-shade` rim, a darker weed ring inside it, then `water-shade` and `water-base` with two flat glint bars. refs/peggys-cove/granite-barrens-and-sea.jpg is a photograph of exactly this.

mustBeRight.feature: glacial erratics sitting ON the pavement, with ground-contact AO
mustBeRight.detail: Four per tile, rounded, in `path-base` with a `path-light` cap and a `path-shade` flank, each on a flat `ao-shadow` ellipse at 0.28. They sit on the rock; they are not part of it.

mustBeRight.feature: board-and-batten fish stores standing on spruce piles OVER the water, with pitched roofs
mustBeRight.why: Sheds on piles over water is what makes this a fishing cove rather than a village beside one.
mustBeRight.detail: Seven per tile in red-oxide, weathered grey and white, each with vertical battens, a gable roof in `slate`, a plank deck and a run of piles below it standing in the water. The red is the `oxide` ramp: red-oxide paint on board-and-batten timber, the same material and the same ramp as the prairie grain elevator's.

mustBeRight.feature: flat mirror reflections of the stores in the cove water
mustBeRight.why: Every reference photograph of this harbour has them and they are what says the water is sheltered.
mustBeRight.detail: Flat vertical bars in each store's own tones, broken by horizontal `water-base` and `water-light` ripple bars. Never a gradient, never a blur (ADR-0011).

mustBeRight.feature: a spruce treeline above the shore, cropped by the tile's own top edge
mustBeRight.detail: Ragged `pine-shade` crowns with `pine-base` catching the key light on the upper left, standing on an opaque band. The crop is deliberate: this tile has to be opaque from its top edge downward, and a treeline whose tops are cut is what a 280 px band of a wooded shore looks like.

the wave texture, foam, weed and reflections of the open sea beyond the cove
every needle and branch: a spruce is a triangle with one lit face
the stores' shingles, hinges, ladders, buoys, traps, ropes and stacked gear
the boats' rigging, aerials, hauling gear, registration numbers and hull names
neverAdd: any recognisable building on either tile. Both repeat, and this level's only place anchor is `peggys-cove-light`
any lettering, sign, hull name, registration number, company name or funnel mark. Every wooden store in the references carries one and this project draws none
a canoe, a kayak or any Indigenous watercraft, as scenery or as anything else (docs/content-review.md 5.4, OQ-REVIEW-10)
an inuksuk or a totem pole, in any form, including background, silhouette and icon (docs/content-review.md 5.2)

a figure of any kind, at any scale, including a silhouette and a crowd. The vancouver seawall draws four unmarked people under section 3.3 outcome 2 and this level deliberately draws none. See assets/style/peggys-cove-level.md section 0
a lighthouse on either tile: it is the POI hero and it may not repeat
snow: this level is a clear Atlantic morning and two of the game's levels are winter already
notes: TWO WATERS ON ONE LEVEL, AND IT IS NOT A MISTAKE. layer-20 is the open Atlantic beyond the mouth of the cove and layer-30 is the sheltered water inside it, which is what Peggy's Cove is: a notch of calm water inside a granite headland, with the ocean on the other side of the rock. The compression is that the two are stacked in one view; the sheet records it rather than leaving it to be found.
The composite is the level's traversal picture and it is where the player spends the whole level. It is never asked for a place.

subjects.subject: A glacial erratic and a tide pool on bare granite barrens
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswer: a boulder resting on bare rock
a large rock on a rocky shore
a rock and a tide pool
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC AND NATURAL. This is a LANDFORM. It names no place, and the gate must not ask it to: the
place-anchor for this level is peggys-cove-light and nothing else.
WHAT IT MUST NOT BE READ AS is the whole reason this subject is written down. If an identifier says
CAIRN, INUKSUK, STACKED STONES, A MARKER or A MONUMENT, that is a FAIL and it is a serious one:
docs/content-review.md forbids all of those in this game outright, and a boulder drawn so that it
reads as one is the exact defect the prohibition exists to prevent. One rounded mass resting on rock,
and a second smaller one beside it, NOT on top of it and NOT balanced on it.

mustBeRight.feature: one large rounded mass resting ON the rock, not growing out of it
mustBeRight.why: That is what an erratic is: a boulder the ice left behind, sitting on pavement it does not belong to. Drawn as an outcrop rising out of the ground it is not this subject, it is a hill.
mustBeRight.detail: A closed rounded silhouette whose foot meets the pavement in a single flat line with a contact shadow under it. Wider than it is tall - MEASURED on peggys-cove/granite-barrens-and-sea.jpg, the boulders in the middle distance run about 1.4 to 1.6 wide to 1 tall, and the shipped art draws 348 x 210 = 1.66. Nothing about it is angular or faceted, because this granite is glacially rounded.

mustBeRight.feature: a second, smaller boulder BESIDE it on the same pavement
mustBeRight.why: One boulder alone reads as scale-less. Two of different sizes on one plane give the eye the ground.
mustBeRight.detail: About half the height of the first, standing clear of it with rock visible between them. NEVER touching, NEVER stacked, NEVER balanced.

mustBeRight.feature: bare pale granite pavement with joint lines and grass only in the joints
mustBeRight.detail: A flat band of `path-light` under everything, with `path-shade` joint lines running through it, and short broken runs of grass tufts that follow a joint and taper at both ends. Bare rock is the subject; grass is what grows in the cracks in it. This matches layer-40-granite-barrens.svg, which the POI stands in front of.

mustBeRight.feature: a shallow tide pool in front, flat and still
mustBeRight.why: It is the second half of what a granite barren is, it is on the reference, and it is what says SEA rather than quarry.
mustBeRight.detail: A flat ellipse of `water-base` inside a `water-shade` rim, with one or two straight `water-light` ripple bars. No reflection of the boulders - a pool this shallow does not carry one at this scale - and no spray.

simplifyAway: lichen, crystal sparkle, grain and mineral speckle: art-bible section 1 forbids a surface pattern, and this rock is where the temptation is worst
the individual joints of the pavement below 12 px
seaweed, barnacles and shells in the pool below 12 px
every erratic beyond the second: the parallax tile behind already carries four
neverAdd: a cairn, an inuksuk, a stone marker, a stacked or balanced stone arrangement of any kind, or any object a viewer could read as one. docs/content-review.md and assets/style/peggys-cove-level.md section 0. This is the single most likely wrong drawing on this subject and it is forbidden outright
a carving, an inscription, a plaque, a painted mark or any lettering

a figure of any kind, at any scale, including a silhouette and a crowd. This level depicts nobody, anywhere - assets/style/peggys-cove-level.md section 0, and the same clause is on both of this level’s original subjects
a flag, a pole, a fence, a bench or any built object: the subject is bare shore
surf, spray, breaking waves or a wet-rock sheen: this level is a clear calm morning and the tide pool is still
notes: WHY A ROCK IS A POINT OF INTEREST. It carries a sourced fact - Discover Canada page 93, the three
oceans, and this is the Atlantic edge - and the brief for this work is explicit that a point of
interest is something a player can stop at and learn one sourced fact from, not necessarily a
landmark. The alternatives considered for this position were a stack of lobster traps and a hauled
dory, and BOTH WERE REFUSED for the same reason: there is no licence-clean photograph of either in
this repository, and this level in particular does not get to invent what it cannot check.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none is set, because there is no identification threshold to protect - a boulder
at 120 px is a boulder. DRAWING OBSERVATION: at 180 px wide the two masses, the light and shade on
each, the joint lines, the grass and the pool are all still legible.

subjects.subject: A red fish store standing on timber cribbing at the water’s edge
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswer: a red shed on a dock
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. There are seven more of these on layer-30-cove.svg, which repeats every 1760 px,
so nothing here may be a named building and nothing may be demanded of it that names one. A verifier
who says "Peggy’s Cove" is not wrong and is not required to, and the gate must not reward it: the
place-anchor for this level is peggys-cove-light.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY: that the building stands OVER WATER on built cribbing. "A red barn", "a house"
or "a cabin" is a FAIL - the cribbing, the deck and the dark water under it are the subject.

mustBeRight.feature: stacked timber cribbing carrying a plank deck, with dark water under it
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes this a fish store and not a shed in a field, and it is the half of the building a photograph of this coast always shows.
mustBeRight.detail: Courses of squared timber laid in a stack between upright posts, drawn in the `glacier` ramp - MEASURED as a pale weathered green on peggys-cove/harbour-and-fish-stores.jpg, which is what that timber goes in salt air - over a `water-shade` field so the gaps between the courses read as shadow and not as sky. The deck is `wood` with a lit cap and a dark underside.

mustBeRight.feature: a red clapboard gable end with white corner trim and white window and door frames
mustBeRight.why: Red with white trim is the colour pair of this coast and it is the whole read at phone size. The Halifax level’s brick is `brick`; this is `oxide`, the same red the seven stores on layer-30-cove.svg already use.
mustBeRight.detail: Walls in `oxide-base` with an `oxide-shade` far end, `white-base` boards at both corners and around every opening. NOT `brick` and NOT `flag-red`.

mustBeRight.feature: a wide plank door facing the deck, big enough to carry gear through
mustBeRight.detail: A double-leaf door about a third of the gable’s width and two thirds of the wall’s height, dark inside its white frame, with one small square window beside it. A domestic front door with a step is a house; this is a working opening.

mustBeRight.feature: a shingled roof drawn as a plain chevron band over the gable
mustBeRight.detail: The gable end faces the player, so the roof is seen as its verge: one band in `slate`, lit on the left slope. No shingle courses, no ridge cap, no eaves detail - art-bible section 1 forbids the pattern and none of it survives 25 per cent anyway.

mustBeRight.feature: a white-railed walkway running to it, and bare granite at its foot
mustBeRight.why: It ties the building to the ground the player is standing on, which is the barrens, and it is what the reference shows.
mustBeRight.detail: A plank walkway on posts entering from one side with a two-rail white handrail, and a band of `path` granite across the bottom of the file. The file’s bottom edge IS the level ground line.

simplifyAway: clapboard boarding and shingle courses: surface pattern, forbidden by art-bible section 1
the lichen on the roof, which is bright orange on the reference and is the strongest single colour in that photograph. It is weather on one building, not a feature of the type
buoys, floats, ropes, nets and gear below 12 px
the individual timbers of the cribbing below 12 px: three courses is the rhythm
reflections in the water under the deck: it is in the building’s own shadow
neverAdd: a sign, a name, a number, a wordmark or any lettering in either language
a lighthouse, a lantern or a light of any kind on this building: this level has exactly one lighthouse and it is the hero

a figure of any kind, at any scale, including a silhouette and a crowd. This level depicts nobody, anywhere - assets/style/peggys-cove-level.md section 0, and the same clause is on both of this level’s original subjects
a lobster trap, a dory or any gear this repository has no reference photograph of. The temptation on this subject is to dress it, and every piece of dressing would be invented
a chimney, a porch, a dormer or a garden: those belong to the house subject and they are what separate the two
notes: peggys-cove/harbour-and-fish-stores.jpg is the PRIMARY reference: it shows the red store, its
cribbing, its deck and its white rail in one frame, with the village houses behind. red-fish-store.jpg
is the second and is a bright-sun exposure, which is where the white trim and the red were checked.
BOTH ARE OF REAL BUILDINGS AND NEITHER IS COPIED. What is drawn is the type: one gable end, one
door, one window, three courses of cribbing. The building in the photograph has a lichened roof, a
lean-to, a second storey door and a jumble of gear, and none of that is here.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw it below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise it.
DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px the cribbing courses, the door, the window,
the corner trim and the rail all survive; the 120 px silhouette is a gabled box standing on legs
over water, which is the subject.

subjects.subject: A clapboard village house behind a picket fence with wild roses
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswer: a house behind a picket fence
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE, like every other built subject on this level except the lighthouse. It is a house.
It names no place and no person and the gate must not ask it to.
WHAT IT MUST CARRY: a HOUSE somebody lives in - the chimney, the domestic windows, the door and the
garden fence. "A barn", "a shed", "a church" or "a store" is a FAIL, and the fence and the roses are
half of why it is not any of them.

mustBeRight.feature: a storey-and-a-half gable end facing the player, with one window in the gable
mustBeRight.why: It is the house form of this coast and it is what makes the building read as a dwelling at a glance: a tall triangle over a short wall, with a window up in the peak where the bedroom is.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on peggys-cove/village-houses.jpg: on the mint-green house the wall below the eave is about 0.55 of the gable’s full height and the roof pitch is close to 40 degrees. The shipped art draws a 340-wide wall 244 tall under a gable rising 122, and one 68 x 72 window centred in the peak.

mustBeRight.feature: white trim against a painted clapboard wall
mustBeRight.why: The colour pair is the whole read at phone size and it is what every house in the reference has. The wall may be any of the village colours; the trim is always white.
mustBeRight.detail: Corner boards at both ends of the wall, a band under the eave, and a white frame around every window and the door. The shipped wall is `felt-light`, the pale yellow of the reference’s second house; `glacier` is the mint green of the first and is used on this file’s door so the two are not the same object.

mustBeRight.feature: a brick chimney standing through the roof slope
mustBeRight.why: A house is heated. It is the one roof feature that separates this from the fish store, whose roof carries nothing at all.
mustBeRight.detail: A plain brick stack with a capping course, passing BEHIND the roof band so it is clearly through the slope rather than sitting on it. `brick`, which no other object on this level uses.

mustBeRight.feature: a weathered picket fence across the front, with wild rose bushes growing over it
mustBeRight.why: It is the garden, it is on every reference of this village, and it is what says somebody lives here rather than works here.
mustBeRight.detail: Pointed pickets of even width and gap on two rails, in weathered `path` tones rather than white - MEASURED on peggys-cove/village-houses.jpg, where the fence is bare silvered wood and the house trim beside it is white, and drawing both white loses the fence. Rosa rugosa bushes in `pine` with rounded pink and red flowers; the bushes break the fence line and stand taller than it in two places.

mustBeRight.feature: it stands on turf, and the turf is the only green ground on this level
mustBeRight.detail: A narrow `grass` band at the very bottom of the file, which is the level ground line. Everywhere else the player walks on `path-light` granite, so this band is what says garden.

simplifyAway: clapboard boarding, shingle courses and the fence’s grain: surface pattern, forbidden by art-bible section 1
sash glazing bars beyond one cross per window
the overhead wires, the satellite dish, the propane tank and the outbuildings in the reference
individual rose leaves and buds: a rounded mass of two greens with flat flower discs on it
the second and third houses of the reference: one house is the subject
neverAdd: a street number, a name board, a mailbox with lettering, a sign or any lettering in either language
a flag, a coat of arms, a wordmark or a decorative emblem on the gable

a figure of any kind, at any scale, including a silhouette and a crowd. This level depicts nobody, anywhere - assets/style/peggys-cove-level.md section 0, and the same clause is on both of this level’s original subjects
a lighthouse, a fishing store, a boat, a net or a trap: this is the dwelling, and every one of those belongs to a different subject on this level
a cross, a steeple or a bell: a white-trimmed gable with a peak window is one wrong addition away from a chapel
notes: peggys-cove/village-houses.jpg is the PRIMARY reference and carries everything on this subject:
three houses, the fence, the roses, the shingle roofs and the brick chimney in one frame. It is a
flat overcast exposure - the sky in it is a grey field - so it is a GEOMETRY AND ARRANGEMENT
reference and the colours are taken from palette.json, lit for the clear morning this level is set on.
NO HOUSE IN THE PHOTOGRAPH IS COPIED. The drawing takes the form from the mint-green house, the wall
colour from the yellow one and the fence and roses from the foreground, and it is one building where
the reference has three.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw it below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise it.
DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px the chimney, the gable window, the two sash
windows, the door, the fence pickets and the roses all survive; the 120 px silhouette is a gabled
house with a chimney behind a fence, which is the subject.

subjects.subject: A Yukon River sternwheeler: a long, low, white, three-deck river freighter with a large ochre paddlewheel at the stern, four tall black hog posts and their truss rods, one tall ochre smokestack and a small white pilot house forward, standing on a gravel bar.
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`. The file is 2300 x 700 since 2026-09-16 — the authored 920 x 280 geometry under one uniform scale(2.5) group, so every ratio measured below is unchanged and this recipe is unaffected — and the vessel's keel is its bottom edge, so there is no empty band: it stands on the ground rather than floating like five-sails' pier. THE FILE IS NOW WIDER THAN THE GAME'S CAMERA (1080 px), so the level shows about half of it at the point a player stops, and the paddlewheel is passed on the walk in rather than framed at the stop. That is stated because it changes NOTHING about this contract, which is judged on the whole rasterised file: a blind verifier still sees the entire vessel. assets/style/the-north-level.md section 13 records why the vessel was rescaled and why a larger scale was refused.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: A TYPE, NOT A PLACE, AND THAT IS THE FINDING RATHER THAN THE DESIGN. This is a specific, cited, existing
National Historic Site vessel, and it is asked only for what it is. The reason is the reason the prairie
grain elevator ships blank: the vessel carries its OWN NAME in large black letters across the bow and
again across the pilot house in every one of the five references, that name is the single most
identifying thing in those photographs, and make verify-art refuses a text element in a render source.
So it ships nameless, and a verifier cannot be asked for a name that is not drawn.
THE CONSEQUENCE IS STATED IN FULL: the North as a PLACE rests on nothing in this level's art. That is
the third region in a row to land there - prairie-rail and alberta-foothills are the first two - and it
is OQ-SPINE-6's finding confirmed a third time rather than a new surprise. The level's answer to `where`
is its territorial statement, its title and its question bank, none of which is a picture.
WHAT THIS RENDER DOES CLAIM is that a paddle steamer is unmistakable as a paddle steamer: a stern wheel
1.8 hull depths across, hog posts taller than the funnel, and a hull 9.7 hull depths long are a shape
nothing else in this game will draw. A verifier who cannot name the TYPE is reporting a defect.

mustBeRight.feature: the paddlewheel is at the STERN and is 1.8 hull depths across
mustBeRight.why: A wheel at the side is a different vessel and a small wheel is a toy. The size of this wheel is the identification.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on refs/the-north/sternwheeler-broadside.jpg with the hull depth - main deck y495 to keel y600 - as the denominator: the wheel spans about 190 px against 105 = 1.80. Drawn 154 across against a hull depth of 86 = 1.79. It is an OPEN wheel - a rim, eight spokes, eight bucket boards and a hub - never a solid disc and never a boxed housing.

mustBeRight.feature: four tall black hog posts, taller than the funnel, with truss rods running to the hull ends
mustBeRight.why: This is what makes it a shallow-draught RIVER boat rather than a coastal steamer, and it is the most graphic thing on the vessel after the wheel.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED: the tallest posts stand about 203 px above the deck against a hull depth of 105 = 1.93, and the funnel reaches 1.81. Drawn 166 against 86 = 1.93. The rods are straight lines from the post heads down to the bow and the stern, drawn OVER the deckhouse because on the vessel they run outboard of it.

mustBeRight.feature: one funnel, not two
mustBeRight.why: Two funnels is the Mississippi showboat this vessel is constantly mistaken for.
mustBeRight.detail: A single ochre stack with a dark cap, aft of the pilot house, in the `wood` ramp. MEASURED at hsl(26,63%,42%) over the reference's saturated ochre against wood-base's hsl(30,52%,39%).

mustBeRight.feature: a long, low, white hull carrying two rows of openings
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED: the whole vessel is about 9.7 hull depths long. A row of small square windows high on the hull and a row of larger freight ports below it, both in the `slate` ramp. The hull is `white`; no outline, per art-bible section 3.

mustBeRight.feature: three white decks stepping inward, with a small pilot house highest and FORWARD
mustBeRight.detail: Main deck house, a shorter saloon deck inset from it, then the pilot house near the bow with a dark roof cap and a short mast. Each deck edge carries a flat ao-shadow band at 0.18 so the stack of white on white separates; the first build had none and the decks merged.

simplifyAway: every stanchion, davit, ladder, capstan, hatch and ventilator on three decks
the wheel's individual bucket fastenings, its cranks, its pitman arms and its shaft bearings
the rigging beyond four truss rods and two stays: the references carry several dozen wires
the cradle, the chocks and the dry berth the vessel actually stands in
the draught marks on the bow and the trim scale on the stern
neverAdd: any lettering, name board, number or draught mark. The vessel carries its own name twice in every reference and this project draws no text anywhere
a second funnel, a side wheel, a bowsprit or a gilded pilot-house crown: this is a working freighter, not a showboat
smoke, steam or a wake: the vessel is on land and nothing in this game draws particles into a render source
a flag: one flies on a POLE ON THE SHORE in the primary reference and it is not part of the vessel
an inuksuk or a totem pole, in any form, including background, silhouette and icon (docs/content-review.md 5.2)
a qamutiik, a dogsled, a dog team, a kayak or a canoe, as scenery, as cargo or as anything else (docs/content-review.md 5.4, OQ-REVIEW-10)
a figure of any kind, at any scale, including a silhouette and a crowd. See assets/style/the-north-level.md section 0
notes: LICENCE FIRST. The Commons API was queried before anything was downloaded and returned CC0, CC BY 2.0 and CC BY 3.0 files of the broadside, the stern quarter, the wheel, the bow and the pilot house. Nine files were taken for this level: two CC0, one CC BY 3.0 and six CC BY 2.0. No ShareAlike file was used (ADR-0004).

THIS LEVEL DEPICTS NO NATION AND NO PERSON, and its territorial fact is quoted from the published words of the one nation it names. The Tier 3 obligation that leaves open is written as a dated obligation in assets/style/the-north-level.md section 0.

subjects.subject: A pale glacier-fed river running between a wall of black spruce on a tan cut bank and a near cobble bar carrying driftwood, willow and sedge.
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the bar drawn OVER the far bank, which is the order the level uses. The bar tile's top edge is 140 px BELOW the far-bank tile's top edge (world y 960 against 820): `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'bank', nearMatch: 'bar', nearTop: 140 })`. Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1760 and 1920). The composite is 460 rows: the far bank occupies 0..150 and the bar 140..460, overlapping by 10. THE SEAM CLOSES TO THE PIXEL: the bar tile is opaque from its own top edge, because its top rows are water, which is the same property that closes vancouver-seawall's seam and for the same reason.
expectedBlindAnswer: a spruce forest above a river
a gravel bar on a river
a river in the boreal forest
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. Both tiles repeat - 1760 and 1920 - so neither may carry anything recognisable: the
spruce, the aspen, the cut bank, the driftwood, the willow and the cobbles are all types. A verifier who
names a place from these two tiles is reporting a defect.
EVERY ACCEPTED PHRASE NAMES THE RIVER, and most of them name the forest as well. That is the line this
list draws rather than a preference: without the river this is a gravel pit, and `a rocky shore` and `a
granite shore` are accepted answers of peggys-cove-barrens, whose picture is bare rock and tide pools
with no running water in it. A list that accepted both would stop being able to tell the two apart.
WHAT THE PLACE RESTS ON: nothing. `paddlewheel-riverboat` is asked for a TYPE and never for a place, and
the reason is in its own note. This level's picture answers `what is this` and not `where is this`.

mustBeRight.feature: the water is PALE, desaturated and green-cyan, not blue
mustBeRight.why: A glacier-fed river carrying rock flour is the one colour that separates this river from the four other waters in this game, and it is why this level added the only new ramp of the day.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on refs/the-north/yukon-river-canyon.jpg: 500x150 of mid-channel at (700,620) has median hsl(176,30%,75%) and 400x110 of near water at (200,760) has median hsl(169,23%,59%). Drawn in the `glacier` ramp, whose base is hsl(172,30%,62%). Three flat tones and straight ripple bars, never a gradient (ADR-0011).

mustBeRight.feature: a WALL of black spruce, narrow and spired, cropped by the tile's own top edge
mustBeRight.detail: Narrow triangles of varying height packed shoulder to shoulder, `pine-base` on the lit left face and `pine-shade` on the right, over an opaque `pine-shade` band. Never rounded broadleaf crowns: a boreal spruce is a spire, and a forest of round trees is a different biome.

mustBeRight.feature: the first gold of autumn in the aspen and willow, and only there
mustBeRight.why: It is what puts the picture in the sub-Arctic in August rather than anywhere in Canada in July, and spread any wider it would turn the boreal forest deciduous.
mustBeRight.detail: Small `brass` crowns tucked among the spruce and one or two lobes on a willow mound. MEASURED at hsl(44,34%,49%) on refs/the-north/yukon-river-bluff-and-aspen.jpg against brass-base's hsl(44,69%,50%); that photograph carries its own fog bank, which is where the saturation went.

mustBeRight.feature: a tan cut bank between the forest and the water
mustBeRight.detail: A `stone` band with vertical gully streaks and a lit crest, and a dark shadow line at the waterline. MEASURED at hsl(43,23%,45%) against stone-base's hsl(36,37%,58%), which is the widest gap that ramp is asked to carry and is recorded in palette.json.

mustBeRight.feature: a cobble bar, with driftwood lying on it
mustBeRight.why: It is the surface the player walks on, and driftwood is what says river rather than beach.
mustBeRight.detail: Flat `path` cobbles getting larger toward the viewer, four bleached driftwood logs each on a flat ao-shadow ellipse at 0.28, willow mounds built from overlapping lobes and clusters of sedge blades. Never sand and never a single flat tone.

simplifyAway: every needle, branch and trunk: a spruce is a triangle with one lit face
the surface texture, foam, standing waves and reflections on the water
the individual stones of the bank beyond a rhythm of cobbles
the willow's leaves and stems: a mound of lobes
the far bank's individual trees beyond the tile's own top edge, which crops them
neverAdd: any recognisable building, vessel or structure on either tile. Both repeat, and the hero is the only non-repeating render on this level
a suspension bridge. One stands in the primary river reference, a hundred metres out of frame of what this level draws, and vancouver-seawall's neverAdd bans the same shape for the same reason
an inuksuk or a totem pole, in any form, including background, silhouette and icon (docs/content-review.md 5.2)
a qamutiik, a dogsled, a dog team, a kayak, a canoe or a fish weir, as scenery or as anything else (docs/content-review.md 5.4, OQ-REVIEW-10)

subjects.subject: A stand of northern spruce on a river bank
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`, the same builder as paddlewheel-riverboat.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE, AND GENEROUS ON SPECIES. "Fir" and "pine" are accepted above even though these are
spruce: nobody identifies a conifer genus from a cartoon at 390 px, and the gate must not pretend
otherwise. What it must NOT be read as is a broadleaf tree, a hedge, a bush or a mountain.
THE SHAPE THAT CARRIES IT IS NARROWNESS. A northern spruce is a spire - much taller than it is wide,
with short drooping tiers - and a wide conical Christmas-tree silhouette belongs to a different forest
and a different latitude. The width : height ratio below is the whole subject.

mustBeRight.feature: narrow spire-topped trees: width no more than about a third of height
mustBeRight.why: It is what separates subarctic white and black spruce from every other conifer a cartoon draws, and it is the read at any size.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on the bank forest in the-north/yukon-river-and-spruce.jpg, where several hundred trees stand in profile against the sky: crown width runs about 0.28 to 0.36 of tree height. The shipped art draws five trees between 0.33 and 0.39 and the tallest at 0.33. A tree at 0.5 or above is a fir from a warmer forest.

mustBeRight.feature: stacked drooping tiers rather than one smooth cone
mustBeRight.detail: Four to seven overlapping triangular tiers per tree, each a little wider than the one above, with a short bare spire at the top. Rhythm, not count.

mustBeRight.feature: five trees of five different heights, overlapping
mustBeRight.why: A row of equal trees is a hedge. Uneven heights are what make a stand.
mustBeRight.detail: Tallest near the centre, shortest at the edges, all standing on the same bank line, each with a short bare trunk showing under its lowest tier.

mustBeRight.feature: three tones of ONE green ramp, lit from the upper left
mustBeRight.detail: The `pine` ramp and nothing else: shade for the body of each tier, base for the lit left face, light for a small highlight on alternate tiers. No autumn colour, no yellow, no dead trees.

mustBeRight.feature: a gravel bank with rounded boulders under them
mustBeRight.detail: A flat band of `path` with a lit crest and two or three rounded boulders, which is the shore this level walks along. The file's bottom edge IS the level ground line.

simplifyAway: individual needles, branches and cones: the tiers are the whole foliage
bark texture and root flare
the hundreds of other trees in the reference: five is the subject
undergrowth, moss and fallen timber: the driftwood is its own subject on this level
neverAdd: an inuksuk or a totem pole, in any form, including background, silhouette and icon (docs/content-review.md 5.2)
a qamutiik, a dogsled, a dog team, a kayak, a canoe or a fish weir, as scenery or as anything else (docs/content-review.md 5.4, OQ-REVIEW-10)
a figure of any kind, at any scale, including a silhouette and a crowd. See assets/style/the-north-level.md section 0
any lettering, sign, marker or cairn of any kind
an aurora, a midnight sun or any night sky: this level is a clear morning

a cabin, a camp, a tent, a fire, a trail, a blaze or anything built or left by anybody. This level depicts no people and no trace of them, and a stand of trees is where a cabin gets drawn without anyone deciding to
a broadleaf tree, autumn colour or a bare trunk: this is a clear-morning evergreen stand
an animal of any kind
notes: the-north/yukon-river-and-spruce.jpg is the PRIMARY reference: a long bank of spruce in profile above
a turquoise river, in full sun. It is the one reference in this set that shows the tree shape clearly
and at a scale where the width-to-height ratio can be measured.
WHY A STAND OF TREES IS A POINT OF INTEREST. It carries a sourced fact - Discover Canada page 103, the
three territories hold a third of Canada's land and about 100,000 people - and the object is the
emptiness that fact is about. This level has no NPC, no building and no figure by design, so the
things a player can stop at are the vessel, the forest and the river's own debris, and that is not a
shortage to be worked around: it is what the level is.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px wide all five trees, the
tier structure and the boulders survive; the 120 px silhouette is five narrow spires of uneven height,
which is a spruce stand and is not a hedge.

subjects.subject: A pile of bleached driftwood on a river gravel bar
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswer: bleached logs on a gravel bar
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC AND NATURAL. It is debris a river left; it names no place and the level's place-anchor is
paddlewheel-riverboat.
THE FAILURE THIS SUBJECT IS WRITTEN AGAINST IS BEING READ AS SOMETHING SOMEBODY BUILT. If an identifier
says A SHELTER, A LEAN-TO, A FIRE, A RAFT, A FISH WEIR, A FENCE, A CAIRN or A MARKER, that is a FAIL
and a serious one: docs/content-review.md forbids several of those outright on this level, and a pile
of logs is one tidy arrangement away from any of them. The logs LIE. None is stood up, leaned against
another, driven into the ground or set in a frame.
A first build's root wad was drawn as an even radial fan and read as a SUNBURST DEVICE. It is now four
uneven roots on one side. An identifier who reports a symbol here has found a defect.

mustBeRight.feature: seven barkless logs LYING across one another at different angles
mustBeRight.why: Lying and crossing is what says the river put them there. Parallel logs read as stacked cordwood, which is something a person does.
mustBeRight.detail: Long capsules with rounded ends, no two at the same angle, none vertical, none steeper than about 20 degrees from the horizontal, overlapping into a low pile no taller than about a third of the longest log.

mustBeRight.feature: bleached pale wood with darker ends
mustBeRight.why: Driftwood is grey-white, not brown. Brown logs with bark are freshly cut timber and that is a different object with a different meaning.
mustBeRight.detail: Bodies in the pale ends of the `path`, `limestone` and `stone` ramps, each log taking all three tones of ONE of them - the light tone for the body, the base tone along the belly, the shade tone for the end face - so every log reads as a lit cylinder rather than a flat lozenge. NO bark, NO green wood, NO axe or saw cuts. `stone` WAS ADDED 2026-09-17, and it is a saturation fix rather than a change of subject. Drawn from `path` and `limestone` alone the pile was six neutral greys end to end: `path` is the one ramp palette.json declares near-neutral and exempts from the saturation gain, so the render breached CLAUDE.md's saturated palette, and it also said less than the truth - sun-bleached driftwood is silver AND warm tan, and `stone` is the warm tan this palette already carries. It is NOT brown: `wood` is the bark-and-fresh-timber ramp, it stays forbidden here, and the reason is this subject's whole point - a brown log with bark is cut timber. A blind pass read the previous build as a stack of cut timber, and the cause was the ARRANGEMENT as much as the colour: all seven logs lay within nine degrees of horizontal in tidy tiers, which is a woodpile. They now span nineteen degrees either side.

mustBeRight.feature: one short uneven root fan
mustBeRight.why: It is what says these were trees the river tore out, rather than milled wood.
mustBeRight.detail: Four roots of different lengths and thicknesses on ONE side of one log's end, spread over less than half a turn, with a small knob at the centre. Never an even radial star.

mustBeRight.feature: a gravel bar with rounded cobbles under it
mustBeRight.detail: A flat band of `path` with a lit crest, a darker foot and four or five rounded cobbles. The file's bottom edge IS the level ground line, which on this level is the bar the player walks along.

simplifyAway: bark, grain, splits and knots
the branches on each log: one root fan on one log is the whole complication
the hundreds of other logs along the shore in the reference
sand ripples, weed and water: the river is a parallax tile behind this
neverAdd: an inuksuk or a totem pole, in any form, including background, silhouette and icon (docs/content-review.md 5.2)
a qamutiik, a dogsled, a dog team, a kayak, a canoe or a fish weir, as scenery or as anything else (docs/content-review.md 5.4, OQ-REVIEW-10)
a figure of any kind, at any scale, including a silhouette and a crowd. See assets/style/the-north-level.md section 0
any lettering, sign, marker or cairn of any kind
an aurora, a midnight sun or any night sky: this level is a clear morning
any arrangement that reads as built: a lean-to, a shelter, a raft, a frame, a fence, a weir, a stack of cordwood, a fire ring or a tripod
a standing or leaning log. Every log lies
an axe, a saw cut, a rope or any tool mark
an even radial root wad, which reads as a sunburst device
notes: the-north/yukon-river-bluff-and-aspen.jpg carries the reference at its waterline: a continuous band of
pale driftwood logs along the foot of the bluff, under autumn aspen. It is a distant, hazy exposure -
the bluff is in fog - so it is a GEOMETRY AND COLOUR-FAMILY reference and nothing finer.
WHY THIS OBJECT CARRIES A GOLD RUSH FACT, which is not obvious and is stated rather than left to look
like a mistake. This level depicts no people, no buildings and no equipment by design, so no object on
it can DEPICT mining. The fact is Discover Canada page 103 - thousands of miners came to the Yukon in
the 1890s and mining is still a significant part of the economy - and it is attached to the object a
player stops at on the river the miners travelled. NOTHING IN THE FILE ASSERTS THE GOLD RUSH: there is
no sluice, no pan, no claim stake and no tool, and the neverAdd list forbids all of them.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: none. DRAWING OBSERVATION, not an identification: at 180 px wide all seven logs, the
darker ends, the root fan and the cobbles survive; the 120 px silhouette is a low crossed pile of
cylinders, which is driftwood and is not a structure.

licenceAudit.method: Wikimedia Commons API, prop=imageinfo&iiprop=extmetadata, before download
licenceAudit.note: Recorded here rather than per asset because credits.schema.json is additionalProperties:false and has no field for a licence-check date. The accepted set widened on 2026-09-08 when the architect reconciled the credits enum with ADR-0004 in both directions: public-domain and CC BY 1.0/2.0/2.5/3.0 added, CC-BY-SA-4.0 removed. Three of the six references parked under OQ-ART-06 became fetchable and are now in; the other three are ShareAlike and stay out. See assets/refs/README.md. Re-run 2026-09-08 for the ten Quebec City references, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded: seven CC0, one public domain (copyright expired, BAnQ), one CC BY 2.0 (Library and Archives Canada) and one CC BY 3.0. Every one is inside the accepted set above. Three ShareAlike candidates that were better photographs - the Dufferin Terrace ice slide in use, the terrace kiosks in winter, and the Chateau after freezing rain - were rejected on licence, not on quality, exactly as three were for Ottawa. Re-run 2026-09-08 for the fifteen Halifax and Toronto references, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded: five CC0, five public domain, three CC BY 2.0, two CC BY 3.0 and one CC BY 4.0. Every one is inside the accepted set above. The Halifax Town Clock's best photographs and every photograph of the Citadel are CC BY-SA and were rejected on licence, not on quality, for the third level running - and for the Town Clock that cost real quality, because the ShareAlike set includes the only high-resolution near-orthographic elevations. The one CC BY 4.0 file that was available carried the day. Re-run 2026-09-08 for the six beaver references, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded: three public domain, one CC0, one CC BY 2.0 and one CC BY 2.5. CC-BY-2.5 appears in this list for the first time and it is inside the enum the architect settled - the intersection in assets/refs/README.md already contained it, and the list above had simply never had a member of it. Re-run 2026-09-13 for ten references for three points of interest that had none, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded, and re-checked against the live API on the same day after an interrupted session: six CC0, two public domain, one CC BY 3.0 and one CC BY 2.0. NONE IS YET ATTACHED TO A SUBJECT, and that is deliberate: checkContract refuses a subject with an empty expectedBlindAnswer or mustBeRight, and those are written by the art agent, not by whoever fetched the photographs. The files are credited in assets/credits.json and listed in assets/refs/README.md. A CORRECTION IS PART OF THIS RECORD. The first pass filtered licences with a pattern that expected 'cc-by-3.0' and the API returns 'CC BY 3.0', so every CC BY file was silently dropped and the pass briefly concluded that no Alberta pump jack was under an accepted licence. That was false, it was caught before anything was committed, and every search below was re-run with a filter tested against 'CC BY 3.0', 'CC BY-SA 4.0', 'CC BY-NC 2.0' and 'CC0'. A licence filter that has not been tested on the strings it will actually see is the ratio-without-a-measured-denominator mistake again. A PUMP JACK: alberta-foothills/pump-jack-foothills-county.jpg (CC BY 3.0, Marek Slusarczyk, Foothills County, Alberta, 2007 - a close side view of a working unit in a fenced lease among hay bales, and the primary reference; its author's required credit line is carried in credits.json), pump-jack-dusk-in-snow.jpg (CC BY 2.0, Damien Goodyear, Alberta, 2015 - a clean side profile under a heavy teal-and-orange grade, so a COLOUR TRAP and a geometry reference only), pump-jack-side-elevation.jpg (public domain by the author's release, a preserved unit in Florida - the whole mechanism near-orthographic) and pump-jacks-on-grassland.jpg (public domain, USDA Forest Service, three working units on a North Dakota grassland pad). Passed over: every other Alberta pump jack on Commons is CC BY-SA (Drayton Valley, Clairmont, Falher, Ponoka, Longview, two 'Ölförderung' and 'Oil Field Pump' Flickr files); 'Alberta IMG 5143' is CC BY 2.0 but carries its author's name burned into the image and shows a distant silhouette the Foothills County file already beats; 'Alberta pumpjack 011' to '013' are public domain but show the machine about 60 px tall. The machine is a TYPE and must never be asked to name a province, exactly as ranch-barn is not. A STREETCAR: toronto/streetcar-flank.jpg, streetcar-beside-older-car.jpg and streetcar-front-and-wires.jpg, all CC0. The best full-length three-quarter view on Commons ('New streetcar 4404 heading south on Spadina, 2014 12 20 (4)') was REJECTED ON LICENCE: its page carries cc-by-sa-2.0 from the Flickr review AND PD-Self under a VRT ticket nobody outside Wikimedia can read, and a file whose own page asserts two licences, one of which is ShareAlike, is not established. NATHAN PHILLIPS SQUARE: toronto/square-arches-and-pool.jpg, city-hall-massing-aerial.jpg and square-winter-rink-and-towers.jpg, all CC0; Canada's freedom of panorama covers the building. 'Curved city hall buildings (Unsplash)' was passed over because its page carries the {{Unsplash}} template rather than an explicit CC0 tag. A POLLING STATION INTERIOR WAS NOT FOUND, and the corrected re-run did not change that. Every Canadian polling-station photograph under an accepted licence shows the outside: signage, doors and the yellow arrow (Raysonho CC0, 2014-2023; ishmael n. daro CC BY 2.0, 2015; Roland Tanglao CC BY 2.0, 2011; Dennis Sylvester Hurd CC BY 2.0, 2019). The 2025 CC BY 2.0 files in the election categories are party yard signs. None shows a voting screen or a ballot box, and all of them are mostly lettering, which this project never draws. The only Canadian ballot boxes under an accepted licence are archive photographs, public domain: 1938 and 1959 (BAnQ) and 1942 (Library and Archives Canada, Mackenzie King at the conscription plebiscite). They show lettered metal and cardboard boxes of that era among identifiable people, no voting screen, and not today's equipment, so they are misses and not finds. Every interior photograph under an accepted licence comes from another country's election (United States, New Zealand, Iceland, Peru, Argentina), and drawing Canada's voting screen from one of them would be invention. ATTACHED 2026-09-13 by the art agent, after the art was drawn: the four pump-jack files to subject pump-jack, the three streetcar files to streetcar, and the three Nathan Phillips Square files to nathan-phillips-square. None was rejected at drawing time. Two findings are recorded on the subjects rather than here: pump-jack-foothills-county.jpg is a rear-fulcrum unit and supplies paint only, and the arches in square-arches-and-pool.jpg span the pool north to south, so they are not drawn. Re-run 2026-09-14 for three references for the Alberta ride, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded, with the licence re-read by the fetch itself: one CC0 (a quarter horse broadside), one CC BY 2.0 (a quarter horse under a western saddle) and one public domain (Muybridge's plate 574, a horse at the walk). The Canadian Horse category on Commons was searched first: six of its nine files are CC BY-SA 3.0 or 4.0 and were rejected on licence. The other three were not used and were not rejected on licence: an 1890s book plate, a CC BY 3.0 show-judging photograph that was not examined, and a CC BY 2.0 photograph of Montreal police horses that carries insignia and identifiable officers. A working quarter horse under a western saddle is what an Alberta ranch horse is. The Bar U Ranch saddle-horse barn photographs are CC BY-SA 4.0.
